gen-1-28: God blessed the first people and gave them the task of filling the earth and caring for it as his representatives. Human life and work have purpose under God's kindness.
gen-1-29: God tells the first people that the plants and fruit of the earth are theirs to eat. From the very beginning, he provides generously for those he made.
gen-3-15: God promised that the woman's descendant would one day crush the serpent, though he would be wounded. Christians have long read this as the first hint of Christ's victory over evil.
gen-8-21: After the flood, God resolved never again to destroy all life in this way, even though human hearts remain bent toward evil. His restraint rests on mercy, not on human goodness.
gen-8-22: God promised Noah that the cycle of seasons, harvests, and day and night would continue as long as the earth lasts. The regular rhythms of nature are a sign of his faithfulness.
gen-9-1: After the flood, God blesses Noah's family and repeats the creation command to have children and fill the earth. Life begins again under his favour.
gen-9-9-11: God made a covenant with Noah, his descendants and every living creature: he would never again destroy the earth with a flood. The promise covers all life, not only Noah's family.
gen-9-12-16: God gave the rainbow as the sign of his covenant never to flood the whole earth again. Whenever it appears, it recalls his lasting commitment to every living thing.
gen-12-2-3: God promised Abram a great nation, a great name and his blessing, so that all peoples on earth would be blessed through him. The New Testament sees this fulfilled through Christ.
gen-12-7: When Abram reached Canaan, God appeared and promised the land to his descendants. Abram answered by building an altar, showing he trusted a promise he would not see fulfilled himself.
gen-13-14-17: After Lot chose the best land, God told Abram to look in every direction: all of it would belong to him and his countless descendants. Abram lost nothing by letting Lot choose first.
gen-15-1: God told Abram not to be afraid, because God himself was his protection and his reward. Abram had refused the spoils of war, and God reminded him that he was better than any plunder.
gen-15-4-5: God promised the childless Abram a son of his own and descendants as countless as the stars. Abram believed him, and God counted his faith as righteousness.
gen-15-13-14: God told Abram that his descendants would be slaves in a foreign land for four hundred years, but he would judge that nation and bring them out with great wealth. Hard times would not cancel his plan.
gen-15-18: God made a formal covenant with Abram, promising his descendants the land from Egypt's river to the Euphrates. God alone passed between the pieces, binding himself to keep it.
gen-16-10: Through his angel, God promised Hagar, a runaway servant, that her descendants would be too many to count. God noticed and cared for someone others had mistreated.
gen-17-4-8: God promised Abraham that he would be the father of many nations and kings, and that the covenant and the land of Canaan would pass to his descendants. His new name, Abraham, marked that promise.
gen-17-15-16: God promised Abraham that his elderly wife, now renamed Sarah, would bear him a son and become the mother of nations and kings. The blessing included her personally.
gen-17-19: God told Abraham that Sarah would have a son named Isaac, and that the everlasting covenant would continue through Isaac's line rather than through Ishmael.
gen-17-20: God promised Abraham that he had heard his prayer for Ishmael: Ishmael too would be blessed, have twelve princes as sons and become a great nation, though the covenant would pass through Isaac.
gen-18-10: The LORD, visiting Abraham, promised that Sarah would have a son by the same time next year. Sarah overheard from the tent and found it hard to believe at her age.
gen-18-14: When Sarah laughed, God asked whether anything is too hard for him and repeated that she would have a son at the appointed time. Human limits do not limit God.
gen-21-12: God told the distressed Abraham to agree to send Hagar and Ishmael away, because his promised family line would come through Isaac. God's purpose guided even a painful household decision.
gen-21-17-18: God heard the cry of Hagar's son in the desert and promised, through his angel, to make Ishmael a great nation. He saw and cared for the outcasts.
gen-22-17-18: After Abraham's willingness to offer Isaac, God swore to bless him, multiply his descendants and bless all nations through his offspring. The New Testament links this offspring to Christ.
gen-26-3-4: During a famine, God told Isaac to stay in the land and promised to be with him, bless him and keep the oath he had sworn to Abraham. The promise passed to the next generation.
gen-26-24: After quarrels over wells, God appeared to Isaac at night, told him not to fear and promised his presence and blessing for Abraham's sake. Isaac responded by worshipping there.
gen-28-13-15: As Jacob fled from Esau, God promised in a dream to give him the land, countless descendants and his constant protection until every promise was kept. Jacob had not earned this grace.
gen-31-3: God told Jacob to leave Laban and return home, promising to be with him on the journey. Jacob's safety rested on that promise, not on his own schemes.
gen-35-10-12: God confirmed Jacob's new name, Israel, and passed on to him the promises made to Abraham and Isaac: many descendants, kings and the land. The nation of Israel takes its name from this moment.
gen-46-3-4: As the elderly Jacob prepared to move to Egypt, God told him not to fear: he would go with him, make his family a great nation there and later bring them back.
gen-48-21: The dying Jacob assures Joseph that God will be with him and bring the family back to Canaan. His hope rests on God's earlier promises rather than on his own presence.
gen-50-24: At the end of his life in Egypt, Joseph assures his brothers that God will come to their aid and lead them to the land promised to their ancestors. He dies trusting that promise.
exo-3-7-8: At the burning bush, God told Moses he had seen Israel's suffering in Egypt and had come to rescue them and bring them to a good land. He does not ignore his people's pain.
exo-3-12: When Moses felt unfit to confront Pharaoh, God promised to be with him. The sign would come afterwards: Israel would worship God on the same mountain.
exo-3-14: God reveals his name to Moses as "I AM WHO I AM". He exists by himself, never changes and depends on no one, so his people can rely on him completely.
exo-4-12: Moses protested that he was a poor speaker, so God promised to help him speak and to teach him what to say. The task came with God's help to carry it out.
exo-6-2-8: God reminded Moses of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and promised to free Israel from slavery, take them as his own people and bring them into Canaan.
exo-12-13: God promised the Israelites in Egypt that when he saw the lamb's blood on their doorframes, he would pass over them and spare them from the final plague. Christians see this as a picture of Christ's sacrifice.
exo-14-13-14: Trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea, the Israelites panicked. Moses told them to stop being afraid and stand firm, because the LORD himself would fight for them that day.
exo-15-2: After crossing the sea, Moses and Israel sing that the LORD is their strength and salvation. They praise the God their ancestors worshipped, who has now rescued them.
exo-15-13: In their song after the sea crossing, the Israelites praise God for leading the people he rescued with faithful love and guiding them toward the place where he lives.
exo-15-26: At Marah, God promised Israel that if they listened to him and kept his commands, he would not bring Egypt's diseases on them, because he is the LORD who heals.
exo-16-4: When Israel was hungry in the desert, God promised Moses he would send bread from heaven each day. Gathering only a day's portion would test whether they trusted and obeyed him.
exo-16-12: God heard Israel's complaints in the desert and promised meat in the evening and bread in the morning, so that they would know he is the LORD their God.
exo-19-4-6: At Sinai, God reminded Israel how he had carried them out of Egypt and promised that, if they kept his covenant, they would be his treasured people, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
exo-20-2: Before giving the Ten Commandments, God reminds Israel who he is: their God, who freed them from slavery in Egypt. His commands follow his rescue; they are not the way to earn it.
exo-20-5-6: In the second commandment, God warns that he will not share worship with idols, and he contrasts limited punishment with faithful love to thousands of generations of those who love and obey him.
exo-20-12: God commands Israel to honour their parents and attaches a promise of long life in the land he was giving them. Paul later calls this the first commandment with a promise.
exo-23-20-22: God promised Israel an angel to guard them on the journey and lead them to the place he had prepared. If they obeyed his guide, God would oppose their enemies.
exo-23-25-26: God promised Israel that if they worshipped him alone, he would bless their food and water, remove sickness, prevent miscarriage and give them full lives in the land.
exo-23-29-30: God told Israel he would drive out the nations of Canaan gradually, not in one year, so the land would not become wild before they were numerous enough to fill it. His timing protected them.
exo-29-45-46: God promised to live among the Israelites and be their God. The purpose of rescuing them from Egypt was this relationship: that they would know him and he would dwell with them.
exo-33-14: After the golden calf, Moses pleaded with God not to abandon Israel. God promised that his presence would go with Moses and that he would give him rest.
exo-33-17: God agreed to Moses' request to keep going with Israel, because Moses had found favour with him and God knew him personally. Moses' intercession was heard.
exo-33-19: When Moses asked to see God's glory, God promised to let his goodness pass by and proclaim his name. His mercy is freely given, not earned or controlled by anyone.
exo-34-6-7: God describes himself to Moses as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and full of faithful love, forgiving sin, yet not ignoring guilt. Later scripture quotes this description often.
exo-34-10: Renewing the covenant after the golden calf, God promised Israel that he would do wonders never seen among any nation, so that everyone around them would see his work.
lev-26-3-6: God promised Israel that if they followed his laws, he would send rain in season, give abundant harvests and grant peace and safety in the land. These were covenant blessings for the nation.
lev-26-9-12: God promised obedient Israel fruitfulness, plentiful food and, above all, his own presence: he would live among them, walk with them and be their God.
lev-26-13: God reminds Israel that he is the one who broke their yoke of slavery in Egypt and let them walk with heads held high. Their freedom was his gift and the basis of the covenant.
lev-26-40-42: God promised that if Israel, scattered for their sin, confessed it and humbled their hearts, he would remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham. Repentance opens the way back.
lev-26-44-45: God promised that even when Israel was in enemy lands under judgment, he would not reject them completely or break his covenant. He would remember the promises made to their ancestors.
num-6-24-26: God gave Aaron's priests these words to bless Israel: asking that the LORD protect them, look on them with favour and grace, and give them peace. It is a prayer God himself authorised.
num-10-33-34: As Israel left Sinai, the ark went ahead to find them a place to rest and the LORD's cloud covered them by day. The story shows God guiding and sheltering his people on the journey.
num-14-17-19: After Israel refused to enter Canaan, Moses pleads with God to show his power by forgiving them. He appeals to God's own description of himself as slow to anger and rich in love.
num-14-20-21: God answered Moses' prayer by pardoning Israel, yet he swore that his glory would fill the earth. Forgiveness did not remove the consequences: that generation would not enter the land.
num-15-40-41: God tells Israel to wear tassels on their clothes as reminders to obey his commands and be holy. He repeats that he is the LORD who freed them from Egypt to be their God.
num-21-8-9: When snakes struck the camp, God told Moses to raise a bronze snake on a pole: anyone bitten who looked at it would live. Jesus later used this as a picture of his cross.
num-23-19-20: Hired to curse Israel, Balaam has to admit that God is not like humans, who lie or change their minds. What God has promised he will do, so Balaam cannot reverse God's blessing.
num-23-21: In his oracle, Balaam declares that God does not view Israel as a people to be condemned, because the LORD is with them and is honoured among them as their king.
num-24-5-7: Looking down on Israel's camp, Balaam describes the people as beautiful and thriving, like well-watered gardens and trees. He foresees their growth and a powerful king.
num-24-17: Balaam foresees a distant ruler rising from Israel like a star, who would defeat Israel's enemies. This was fulfilled partly in David, and Christians have also linked it to the Messiah.
deu-1-29-31: Moses recalls how he urged the frightened Israelites not to fear the people of Canaan, because God had fought for them in Egypt and carried them through the desert like a father carries his son.
deu-2-7: Moses reminds Israel that during forty years in the desert, God blessed their work, watched over their journey and was with them, so that they lacked nothing they needed.
deu-4-7: Moses tells Israel that no other nation has a god as near to them as the LORD is whenever they pray. Their privilege was a God who listens when they call.
deu-4-29-31: Moses promised Israel that even if they were scattered among the nations, they would find God when they sought him wholeheartedly, because he is merciful and will not forget his covenant.
deu-4-39-40: Moses urges Israel to grasp that the LORD alone is God in heaven and on earth, and to keep his commands so that life would go well for them and their children in the land.
deu-5-9-10: In the Ten Commandments, God forbids worshipping idols and warns of the consequences for those who hate him, while promising faithful love to thousands who love him and keep his commands.
deu-5-29: God expresses his longing that Israel would have hearts that truly revere him and obey him always, so that things would go well with them and their children for ever.
deu-6-4-5: Moses declares Israel's central confession: the LORD alone is God. He calls the people to love God with everything they have. Jesus later called this the greatest commandment.
deu-7-6-8: Moses explains that God chose Israel as his own people, not because they were large or impressive, but simply because he loved them and kept the oath he had sworn to their ancestors.
deu-7-9: Moses tells Israel to know that the LORD is the faithful God, who keeps his covenant and steadfast love for a thousand generations of those who love him and obey him.
deu-7-12-13: Moses promised Israel that if they kept God's laws, God would keep his covenant love, bless their families, crops and herds, and increase their numbers in the land.
deu-7-15: Moses assured Israel that, as part of the covenant blessings, God would keep them from the terrible diseases they had seen in Egypt. It was a promise to the nation in the land.
deu-8-2-4: Moses tells Israel to remember how God led them through the desert to humble and test them. He let them hunger and then fed them with manna, teaching them to live by his word.
deu-8-7-10: Moses told Israel that God was bringing them into a rich land of water, grain, fruit and minerals where they would lack nothing. When they had eaten and were satisfied, they should thank God.
deu-8-15-16: Moses reminds Israel that God led them through a dangerous desert, gave water from rock and fed them with manna. The hardship was meant to humble them and do them good in the end.
deu-9-3: Moses assures Israel that the LORD would go ahead of them like a consuming fire and defeat the strong nations of Canaan. Victory would come from God, not from their own strength.
deu-10-12-13: Moses sums up what God asks of Israel: to revere him, walk in his ways, love and serve him wholeheartedly and keep his commands. These requirements were given for their own good.
deu-10-17-19: Moses describes the LORD as the supreme God who cannot be bribed, defends orphans and widows and loves foreigners. Israel must love foreigners too, since they were once foreigners in Egypt.
deu-11-11-12: Moses tells Israel that, unlike Egypt, Canaan depends on rain, and that God himself cares for that land and watches over it all year round. Their harvests would depend on his care.
deu-11-18-21: Moses tells Israel to fix God's words in their hearts, teach them to their children and talk about them every day, so that their families would live long in the land.
deu-11-26-28: Moses sets before Israel a blessing and a curse: blessing if they obey God's commands, and a curse if they turn away to follow other gods. The choice was theirs to make.
deu-12-9-10: Moses told Israel that they had not yet reached the rest God was giving them, but once they crossed the Jordan, God would give them peace from their enemies and they would live safely.
deu-15-4-6: Moses promised that if Israel obeyed God fully, God would bless them so richly that no one need stay poor among them. They would lend to many nations and not need to borrow.
deu-18-15-18: Moses promised Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him, who would speak God's words. The New Testament sees this ultimately fulfilled in Jesus.
deu-20-1-4: Moses tells Israel not to fear stronger armies in battle, because the God who brought them out of Egypt would be with them. The priest was to remind the soldiers that God fights for them.
deu-23-5: Moses reminds Israel that God refused to listen to Balaam and turned his curse into a blessing for them, simply because he loved them.
deu-23-14: Moses tells Israel to keep their camp clean because God moves among them to protect them and give them victory. His presence called for holiness in everyday life.
deu-26-17-19: Moses describes the covenant as a two-way commitment: Israel declared that the LORD is their God, and God declared them his treasured people, to be honoured and holy.
deu-28-1-6: Moses promised Israel that if they obeyed God faithfully, he would raise them above the nations and bless every part of life: city and field, family and herds, food, coming and going.
deu-28-7-8: Moses promised obedient Israel that God would defeat their attackers and bless their barns and all their work in the land. These were national covenant blessings, not a private guarantee.
deu-28-11-12: Moses promised that God would give obedient Israel plenty of children, livestock and crops, and send rain from his storehouse in the sky. They would lend to nations rather than borrow.
deu-30-1-3: Moses foretold that after blessing and curse, if scattered Israel returned to God and obeyed him with all their heart, he would have compassion and gather them back from the nations.
deu-30-4-6: Moses promised that God would bring Israel back from even the farthest places and change their hearts, so they would love him completely and live.
deu-30-8-10: Moses promised that when Israel turned back and obeyed, God would again delight in doing them good and make their families, livestock and fields prosper, as he did for their ancestors.
deu-30-11-14: Moses insists that God's command is not too hard or far away. They need not go to heaven or across the sea to find it; it is already known, in their mouths and hearts. Paul echoes this in Romans 10.
deu-30-15-16: Moses tells Israel that he has set before them life and good, death and harm. Loving God and keeping his ways would lead to life and blessing in the land.
deu-30-19-20: Moses calls heaven and earth to witness and urges Israel to choose life by loving God, obeying him and holding fast to him. God himself is their life.
deu-31-6: Before his death, Moses tells Israel to be strong and courageous as they enter Canaan, because God himself would go with them and never abandon them. Hebrews 13:5 applies this to believers.
deu-31-8: Moses encourages Joshua, his successor, that the LORD would go ahead of him, stay with him and never leave him, so he need not be afraid or discouraged.
deu-32-9-10: In his song, Moses describes Israel as God's own treasured portion. God found them in a barren desert, surrounded them with care and guarded them like the pupil of his eye.
deu-32-11-12: Moses compares God to an eagle that stirs its nest and catches its young on its wings. God alone led Israel; no foreign god helped them.
deu-32-36: Moses' song foretells that God would judge his people's sin, yet show compassion when he saw their strength completely gone. His mercy meets them at their weakest point.
deu-32-39: In Moses' song, God declares that he alone is God. He brings death and life, wounds and heals, and no one can rescue anyone from his hand.
deu-33-12: In his final blessing, Moses describes Benjamin as loved by the LORD and living securely with him, sheltered by God all day long.
deu-33-26-27: Moses praises the God of Israel, who rides the heavens to help them. The eternal God is their refuge and holds them up with everlasting arms.
deu-33-29: Moses ends his blessings by calling Israel happy, a people rescued by the LORD, who is their shield and their sword. Their security came from God, not their own power.
jos-1-3-5: God promised Joshua the land he would set foot on and assured him that no one would stand against him. As he had been with Moses, he would be with Joshua and never abandon him.
jos-1-6-7: God commands Joshua to be strong and courageous, because he would lead Israel into the land. Above all, he must carefully obey the law Moses gave, without turning aside.
jos-1-8-9: God told Joshua to keep his law in mind day and night and obey it, so he would succeed in leading Israel. He also promised to be with Joshua wherever he went. Living by God's word still matters today.
jos-3-7: God promised Joshua that from that day he would honour him before Israel, so the people would know that God was with Joshua as he had been with Moses.
jos-6-2: Before the battle, God told Joshua that he had already given Jericho, its king and its soldiers into his hands. Victory was God's gift before a single wall fell.
jos-10-8: As the southern kings attacked, God told Joshua not to fear them, because he had handed them over and none would be able to stand against him.
jos-14-9: Caleb reminds Joshua that Moses had sworn to give him the land he walked on, because Caleb followed the LORD wholeheartedly. Now, at eighty-five, he asks to receive it.
jos-21-43-45: The writer records that God gave Israel the whole land he had sworn to their ancestors and granted them rest. Not one of his good promises to Israel failed; every one came true.
jos-23-10-11: In his farewell, Joshua reminds Israel that one of them could rout a thousand because God fought for them. He urges them to be careful to keep loving the LORD.
jos-23-14: Near death, Joshua tells Israel that they know in their hearts that not one of God's good promises to them had failed. Every one had been fulfilled.
1sa-2-1-2: After God answered her prayer for a son, Hannah sings with joy. She praises the LORD as holy and unique, a rock like no other, who has rescued her.
1sa-2-6-8: In her song, Hannah praises God as the one who controls life and death, poverty and wealth. He lifts the poor and needy from the dust and gives them honour.
1sa-2-9-10: Hannah declares that God guards the steps of his faithful people while the wicked fall silent, since no one wins by strength. She ends with hope for God's anointed king.
1sa-7-12: After God gave Israel victory over the Philistines, Samuel set up a stone named Ebenezer, meaning that the LORD had helped them all the way to this point.
1sa-12-22: Samuel assures Israel, who had sinned by demanding a king, that God would not abandon them, for the sake of his own name and because he had chosen them as his people.
1sa-16-7: When Samuel was impressed by Eliab's appearance, God told him that he does not judge as people do: they look at the outside, but God looks at the heart.
2sa-7-8-11: Through Nathan, God reminded David that he had taken him from shepherding to be king, and promised him a great name, a secure home for Israel and a lasting dynasty.
2sa-7-12-13: God promised David that a son of his would succeed him, build God's temple and have a kingdom established for ever. Christians see the final fulfilment in Jesus, the son of David.
2sa-7-14-16: God promised to be a father to David's heir. He would discipline him when he sinned but never withdraw his faithful love, and David's house and throne would endure for ever.
2sa-22-2-4: After being rescued from his enemies and from Saul, David praises God as his rock, fortress, shield and saviour. He called on the LORD and was saved.
2sa-22-29-31: David praises God as the lamp who lights his darkness and gives him strength to face any enemy. God's way is perfect, his word proves true, and he shields all who trust him.
2sa-22-33-34: David praises God as his strong refuge, who made his path secure and gave him sure feet, like a deer's, to stand safely on the heights.
1ki-3-12-14: Because Solomon asked for wisdom to govern rather than wealth, God promised him unmatched wisdom plus riches and honour, and long life if he obeyed as David had.
1ki-6-12-13: While Solomon built the temple, God promised that if he obeyed, God would keep his promise to David and live among Israel without abandoning them. A building alone was not enough.
1ki-8-56: At the temple's dedication, Solomon praises God for giving Israel rest, as he had promised. Not one word of all the good promises given through Moses had failed.
1ki-9-3: God told Solomon that he had heard his prayer and consecrated the temple. His name, his eyes and his heart would be there, though later verses make this depend on faithfulness.
2ki-6-16: Surrounded by an enemy army, Elisha tells his frightened servant that those on their side outnumber the enemy. Then God opens the servant's eyes to see an army of fire.
2ki-19-30-31: During the Assyrian siege, God promised through Isaiah that a surviving remnant of Judah would take root again and flourish. God's own zeal would make it happen.
2ki-20-5: When King Hezekiah was dying, God sent Isaiah to tell him that he had heard his prayer and seen his tears, and would heal him so that he could go up to the temple in three days.
1ch-16-34: When the ark was brought to Jerusalem, Israel was called to thank the LORD because he is good and his faithful love lasts for ever. This refrain echoes throughout scripture.
1ch-17-11-14: God promised David that he would raise up one of his sons, who would build God's house and whose throne God would establish for ever in God's own kingdom.
1ch-28-20: David encourages Solomon to be strong and get on with building the temple, because the LORD would be with him and not abandon him until the work was finished.
1ch-29-11-12: David praises God because all greatness, power and glory belong to him. Everything in heaven and earth is his, and wealth, honour and strength come from his hand.
2ch-7-14: God promised Israel that if they humbled themselves, prayed and turned from sin, he would forgive them and heal their land. His readiness to forgive those who truly repent still stands.
2ch-7-15-16: God promised Solomon that he would listen to prayers made at the temple. He had chosen and consecrated it, and his name, eyes and heart would be there.
2ch-15-2: The prophet Azariah tells King Asa that the LORD is with them while they stay with him. If they seek God they will find him, but if they abandon him, he will abandon them.
2ch-15-7: Azariah urges Asa and Judah to be strong and not lose heart in their work of reform, because it would be rewarded. Asa responded by removing idols from the land.
2ch-16-9: The seer Hanani rebukes Asa for relying on a foreign king instead of God. God watches the whole earth to strengthen those who are devoted to him, but Asa had acted foolishly.
2ch-20-15-17: Facing a huge invading army, Judah heard God's message through Jahaziel: do not be afraid, the battle is God's. They only had to take their positions and watch him rescue them.
2ch-20-20: As Judah marched out to face their enemies, King Jehoshaphat urged the people to trust the LORD and his prophets. Faith in God would make them stand firm and succeed.
ezr-8-22: Ezra explains that he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers, because he had told him that God's hand is good to those who seek him but against those who abandon him.
ezr-8-31: Ezra records that God's hand was on the returning exiles and protected them from enemies and bandits all the way from the river Ahava to Jerusalem.
neh-1-8-9: Nehemiah prays, reminding God of his word through Moses: unfaithfulness would bring exile, but if the people returned to him, he would gather them back to the place he had chosen.
neh-2-20: When enemies mocked the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, Nehemiah answered that the God of heaven would give them success. His servants would build, and the opponents had no claim there.
neh-8-10: When the people wept on hearing God's law, Nehemiah told them to celebrate and share food with those who had none. It was a holy day, and joy in the LORD would be their strength.
neh-9-17: In Israel's prayer of confession, the Levites admit their ancestors' stubborn rebellion, yet praise God as ready to forgive, gracious, compassionate, patient and full of love.
neh-9-19-21: The Levites recall that God's great mercy did not abandon Israel in the desert. The cloud and fire guided them, his Spirit taught them, and for forty years they lacked nothing.
job-1-21: After losing his children and his wealth, Job worships. He acknowledges that he came into the world with nothing and will leave with nothing, and still blesses the LORD's name.
job-5-17-18: Eliphaz tells Job that the person God corrects is blessed, since God wounds and heals. The idea has truth, but God later says Job's friends did not speak rightly about him.
job-8-20-21: Bildad assures Job that God does not reject the innocent and will again fill him with laughter. He wrongly implies Job's suffering must be punishment, which God later corrects.
job-11-13-15: Zophar urges Job to turn his heart to God and put away sin, so that he could face life without shame or fear. The advice wrongly assumes Job's suffering came from hidden sin.
job-12-9-10: Job answers his friends that all creation knows God's hand is behind everything. The life of every creature and the breath of every person are in God's hand.
job-13-15: Job says that even if God should kill him and he has no hope left, he will still argue his case before God. He keeps turning toward God rather than away.
job-14-14-15: Job wonders whether the dead can live again. He imagines waiting through his hard service until release comes, when God would call and Job would answer, God longing for what he made.
job-16-19: In deep anguish, Job insists that even now he has a witness in heaven who will speak up for him. He looks beyond his accusers to God above.
job-19-25-27: Job declares that he knows his Redeemer lives and will stand on the earth at the end. Even after his body is destroyed, he expects to see God with his own eyes.
job-22-21-23: Eliphaz urges Job to make peace with God, receive his teaching and turn from wrongdoing so that good would come to him. The call is sound, but his accusation of Job was mistaken.
job-23-10: Though he cannot find God, Job is confident that God knows the path he is on. After God has tested him, he believes he will come out like refined gold.
job-23-13-14: Job reflects that God is unique and no one can stop him. He does whatever he wishes and will carry out what he has planned for Job, which leaves Job in awe and fear.
job-33-27-28: Elihu describes a person who confesses their sin and then tells others that God rescued them from the grave, so that they live to see the light. God's discipline aims to restore.
job-36-7: Elihu argues that God never takes his eyes off the righteous and can raise them to honour, like kings on a throne. He speaks of God's care, though Elihu's verdict on Job is mixed.
job-36-15-16: Elihu says God uses suffering to rescue the afflicted and open their ears. He suggests God wanted to lead Job out of distress into freedom and plenty.
job-42-2: Job admits to God that he can do anything and that none of his plans can be stopped. It is a humble confession, not a promise.
job-42-10: The book tells how God restored Job's fortunes and gave him twice as much as before, after Job prayed for the friends who had wronged him.
job-42-12: The book closes by saying God blessed the latter part of Job's life more than the first. The restoration was God's gift, not a reward Job had demanded.
psa-1-1-3: The first psalm describes the happy person who avoids the ways of the wicked and delights in God's law, thinking about it constantly. Such a person is like a well-watered, fruitful tree.
psa-2-7-8: In this royal psalm, the king reports God's decree naming him as God's son and offering him the nations as his inheritance. The New Testament applies these words to Jesus.
psa-3-3-4: Fleeing from his son Absalom, David declares that God is a shield around him, the one who restores his dignity. When he cries out, God answers him.
psa-3-5-6: Even with enemies all around, David lay down, slept and woke safely, because the LORD kept him. He refuses to fear even tens of thousands of opponents.
psa-4-3: David tells those who oppose him that God has set apart the faithful for himself. Because of that, David is confident the LORD hears him when he prays.
psa-4-8: At the end of a troubled day, David says he can lie down and sleep in peace, because God alone keeps him safe. His rest comes from trust, not from his circumstances.
psa-5-11-12: David prays that all who take refuge in God would rejoice and sing for joy under his protection. He is confident that God blesses the righteous and surrounds them with favour like a shield.
psa-8-3-5: Looking at the night sky, David marvels that the Creator of the moon and stars cares about human beings. God has given people great dignity, crowning them with glory and honour.
psa-9-9-10: David praises the LORD as a safe stronghold for the oppressed in times of trouble. Those who know God's character trust him, because he has never abandoned those who seek him.
psa-9-18: David is confident that God will not forget the needy for ever. The hope of the poor may seem lost for a time, but it will not finally come to nothing.
psa-10-17-18: After lamenting that the wicked seem to get away with it, the writer is sure that God hears the humble, strengthens them and defends orphans and the oppressed against those who terrorise them.
psa-11-1: When advisers urge David to flee like a bird to the mountains, he refuses. He has already made the LORD his refuge, so he will not run in panic.
psa-12-5: God promises to rise up because of the suffering of the weak and the groans of the needy, and to keep them safe from those who slander them. He sees their oppression.
psa-14-5-6: David says those who deny God will be overwhelmed with fear, because God sides with the righteous. Fools may mock the plans of the poor, but the LORD is their refuge.
psa-16-8-11: David keeps the LORD always before him and feels secure, glad and at rest, because God will not abandon him to the grave. Peter later applied these words to Jesus' resurrection.
psa-17-8: David asks God to guard him as carefully as the pupil of the eye and to hide him under the shadow of his wings, like a bird protecting its young.
psa-18-1-3: Rescued from Saul and his enemies, David says he loves the LORD and piles up images of safety: rock, fortress, shield and stronghold. He called on God and was saved.
psa-18-30: David declares that God's way is perfect and his word has been tested and found true. He shields everyone who takes refuge in him.
psa-19-7-11: David praises God's law as perfect and trustworthy. It renews the soul, gives wisdom, brings joy and is more valuable than gold. Keeping it brings great reward.
psa-20-6-7: Before battle, the people express confidence that the LORD will save his anointed king. Others rely on chariots and horses, but Israel will trust in the name of their God.
psa-22-24: After crying out that God seemed to have abandoned him, the psalmist praises God for not despising the sufferer's pain. God did not hide but heard his cry. Jesus quoted this psalm on the cross.
psa-22-26-27: The psalm moves from suffering to a vision of the poor eating until satisfied and all nations turning to worship the LORD. Christians see this as the worldwide result of Christ's suffering.
psa-23-1-4: God promises that he will take care of you like a good shepherd takes care of his sheep. You can trust God to meet all of your needs.
psa-23-5-6: David pictures God as a generous host who prepares a feast for him even with enemies watching. He is sure that God's goodness and love will follow him all his life, and he will live with God for ever.
psa-24-3-5: The psalm asks who may come into God's presence and answers: those with clean hands and pure hearts, who reject idols and lies. They receive blessing and vindication from God.
psa-25-8-10: David praises God as good and upright, so he teaches sinners the right way and guides the humble. All his ways are loving and faithful toward those who keep his covenant.
psa-25-14: David says the LORD confides in those who revere him and makes his covenant known to them. Reverence for God leads to close friendship with him.
psa-27-1: David says the LORD is his light, salvation and strength, so he has no reason to be afraid of anyone. His courage rests on who God is.
psa-27-4-5: David's one great desire is to live in God's presence, to see his beauty and seek him. He is confident that God will shelter him and lift him to safety when trouble comes.
psa-27-10: David says that even if his father and mother abandoned him, the LORD would take him in. God's care is more certain than the closest human love.
psa-27-13-14: David is confident that he will see the LORD's goodness in this life. He then urges himself and others to wait for the LORD with strength and courage.
psa-28-6-7: David praises the LORD for hearing his cry for mercy. God is his strength and shield; he trusted him and was helped, so he bursts into thankful song.
psa-28-8-9: David says the LORD is the strength of his people and the refuge of his anointed king. He then prays that God would save, bless and shepherd his people for ever.
psa-29-11: After describing God's powerful voice in the storm, the psalm ends by confidently asking that the LORD give strength to his people and bless them with peace.
psa-30-5: David tells God's people that God's anger lasts only a moment while his favour lasts a lifetime. Weeping may last through the night, but joy comes with the morning.
psa-31-5: David entrusts his life into God's hands, confident that the faithful God will rescue him. Jesus spoke these words on the cross as he died.
psa-31-19-20: David marvels at the goodness God has stored up for those who revere him and take refuge in him. In his presence, God hides them from human plots and accusing tongues.
psa-31-23-24: David calls all God's faithful people to love him, because he protects the faithful and repays the proud. He urges everyone who hopes in the LORD to be strong and take heart.
psa-32-1-2: David describes the deep happiness of someone whose sins God has forgiven and covered, and who no longer counts their guilt against them. Honesty before God is part of that freedom.
psa-32-7-8: God promises, answering David's prayer, that he will teach his people the way they should go. He will guide them with his loving eye watching over them.
psa-33-4-5: The psalmist praises God because his word is right and everything he does is faithful. He loves justice, and the whole earth is full of his unfailing love.
psa-33-18-22: The psalm says God watches over those who revere him and hope in his love, rescuing them from death and famine. The people respond that they wait for him as their help and shield.
psa-34-4-7: David tells how he sought the LORD and was freed from all his fears. Those who look to God are radiant, and the angel of the LORD camps around those who revere him.
psa-34-8: David invites others to taste and see for themselves that the LORD is good. Those who take refuge in him are truly happy. Peter echoes this invitation for believers.
psa-34-15-18: David says God watches the righteous and hears their cries, while opposing evildoers. He is close to the brokenhearted and rescues those whose spirits are crushed.
psa-34-19-22: David admits that the righteous face many troubles, but says the LORD rescues them from all of them. Those who take refuge in him will not be condemned.
psa-35-9-10: David vows that he will rejoice in God's rescue. His whole being will say there is no one like the LORD, who protects the weak from those too strong for them.
psa-36-5-9: David praises God's love as reaching to the heavens and his justice as deep as the sea. People find refuge in his shadow, feast on his abundance and drink from his fountain of life.
psa-37-3-6: David advises those troubled by evildoers to trust the LORD, do good and delight in him. Those who commit their way to God will see him bring their righteousness to light.
psa-37-7-8: David urges readers to be still before the LORD and wait patiently, rather than fretting when wicked people succeed. Anger and worry only lead toward doing wrong.
psa-37-23-24: David observes that the LORD makes firm the steps of a person whose way pleases him. Even if they stumble, they will not fall headlong, because God holds their hand.
psa-37-25-26: Looking back on a long life, David says he has never seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging. It is his observation of God's care, not a guarantee against every hardship.
psa-37-39-40: David concludes that rescue for the righteous comes from the LORD, their stronghold in trouble. He helps and delivers them because they take refuge in him.
psa-39-7: Overwhelmed by how short and fragile life is, David asks what he is waiting for and answers that his only hope is in the Lord.
psa-40-1-3: David tells how he waited patiently for the LORD, who heard him, lifted him out of a pit of mud and set his feet on a rock. God gave him a new song that leads others to trust.
psa-40-11: David asks God not to hold back his mercy, and prays that God's love and faithfulness would always protect him. He is facing troubles too many to count.
psa-41-1-3: David says those who care for the poor are blessed. The LORD will rescue them in trouble, protect them and support them on their sickbed.
psa-42-5: Feeling far from God and downcast, the psalmist questions his own sadness and tells himself to hope in God. He expects that he will yet praise him again.
psa-42-8: In the middle of his distress, the psalmist remembers that the LORD shows his love by day and gives him a song at night, a prayer to the God of his life.
psa-43-3-5: The psalmist asks God to send his light and truth to lead him back to his presence, where he will worship with joy. Again he urges his troubled soul to hope in God.
psa-44-6-8: Israel confesses that they do not trust in their own weapons. It is God who has saved them from their enemies, so they boast in him and thank him continually.
psa-46-1-3: The psalm declares that God is his people's refuge and strength, always ready to help in trouble. So they will not be afraid, even if the earth shakes and the seas rage.
psa-46-10-11: God commands the nations to stop fighting and know that he is God, who will be honoured everywhere. The people respond that the LORD of hosts is with them as their fortress.
psa-47-8-9: The psalm celebrates God as king over all nations, seated on his holy throne. Leaders of the peoples gather as the people of Abraham's God, because he rules supreme.
psa-48-14: After admiring Jerusalem, the psalmist concludes that this God is their God for ever. He will guide his people through life, even to the end.
psa-49-15: Unlike the rich, who cannot buy their way out of death, the psalmist is sure that God will rescue him from the grave and take him to himself.
psa-50-15: God promises his people that when they call on him in trouble, he will rescue them and they will honour him. What he wants is real dependence on him, not more sacrifices.
psa-51-7-12: After his sin with Bathsheba, David begs God to wash him clean, blot out his guilt and create a pure heart in him. He asks for God's Spirit to stay and for the joy of salvation to return.
psa-52-8-9: In contrast to a boastful destroyer, David pictures himself as a flourishing olive tree in God's house. He trusts God's love for ever and will keep thanking him for what he has done.
psa-54-4: Betrayed by people who told Saul where he was hiding, David declares that God is his helper and the Lord is the one who keeps him alive.
psa-55-22: Betrayed by a close friend, David urges readers to hand their burdens over to the LORD, who will hold them up. God will not let the righteous be overthrown for good.
psa-56-3-4: Captured by the Philistines in Gath, David resolves that whenever he is afraid he will trust God. Trusting God's word, he asks what mere humans could really do to him.
psa-56-8: David says God has kept track of all his wanderings and stored his tears as if in a bottle and recorded them in his book. None of his suffering has gone unnoticed.
psa-57-1: Hiding from Saul in a cave, David pleads for mercy and says he will shelter under God's wings, like a young bird, until the danger has passed.
psa-57-2-3: David cries out to God Most High, who carries out his purpose for him. He is confident God will send help from heaven and show his love and faithfulness.
psa-59-9-10: While Saul's men watched his house to kill him, David says he will watch for God, his strength and fortress. God's love will go before him and let him see his enemies defeated.
psa-60-11-12: After a military defeat, David asks God for help, admitting that human help is useless. With God, Israel will fight bravely, because he is the one who will defeat their enemies.
psa-61-1-4: Feeling far away and overwhelmed, David asks God to hear him and lead him to a rock too high for him to reach alone. God has been his refuge, and he longs to live in his tent for ever.
psa-62-1-2: Surrounded by people trying to bring him down, David says he finds rest in God alone. God is his rock, rescue and fortress, so he will not be badly shaken.
psa-62-5-8: David tells himself to rest quietly in God, his only source of hope, and then urges all the people to trust God at all times and pour out their hearts to him.
psa-63-1-4: In the dry desert of Judah, David says he longs for God more than a thirsty body longs for water. God's love is better than life, so he will praise him as long as he lives.
psa-64-10: After God defeats those plotting harm, David says the righteous will rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him, and everyone who is upright in heart will praise him.
psa-65-1-4: David praises God, who hears prayer and forgives the sins that overwhelmed his people. Those he chooses and brings near to live in his courts are truly blessed.
psa-66-8-9: The psalmist calls all peoples to praise God, who has kept his people alive and not let their feet slip through times of testing.
psa-66-16-20: The psalmist invites those who revere God to hear what he did. Had he clung to sin, God would not have listened, but God did hear his prayer and did not withhold his love.
psa-67-1-2: Echoing the priestly blessing, the psalm asks God to be gracious and bless his people, so that his ways and salvation would become known among all nations.
psa-68-5-6: David praises God as father to the fatherless and defender of widows. He gives the lonely a family and leads prisoners out to freedom, while the rebellious live in barren land.
psa-68-19-20: David praises the Lord, who carries his people's burdens day by day. He is a God who saves, and he alone has power to rescue from death.
psa-69-13: Mocked and in deep trouble, David turns to God in prayer at a time of God's favour. He asks God to answer him out of his great love and faithful salvation.
psa-69-32-33: David says the poor will see God's rescue and be glad, and those who seek God will be encouraged, because the LORD hears the needy and does not ignore his people in captivity.
psa-70-4-5: David prays that all who seek God would rejoice in him. Then he admits that he himself is poor and needy, and begs God, his helper and rescuer, to come quickly.
psa-71-5-6: An older believer tells God that he has been his hope and confidence since youth. He has depended on God since birth and will always praise him.
psa-71-14-16: The ageing psalmist resolves to keep hoping and to praise God more and more. He will tell of God's saving acts all day, though they are too many to measure.
psa-71-20-21: The psalmist admits God has let him see many bitter troubles, yet he is confident God will restore his life, bring him up from the depths and comfort him again.
psa-72-12-14: This prayer for the king describes the ideal ruler, who rescues the needy, pities the weak and treats their lives as precious. Christians see this ideal fulfilled in Christ's reign.
psa-72-17-19: The royal psalm prays that the king's name would last for ever and all nations would be blessed through him. It closes by praising the God of Israel, whose glory should fill the earth.
psa-73-23-26: After nearly losing his faith out of envy of the wicked, Asaph realises God has held his hand all along. God guides him now and will take him into glory; God is all he needs.
psa-73-28: Asaph concludes that, unlike those who drift from God, he finds it good to be near God. He has made the Lord his refuge and wants to tell of all his works.
psa-77-11-14: In sleepless distress, Asaph decides to remember God's wonders of old and think deeply about them. He concludes that no god is as great as the God who works miracles.
psa-80-3: In a time of national disaster, the psalm prays that God would restore his people and let his face shine on them, so that they would be saved.
psa-80-18-19: The people promise not to turn away from God again if he revives them. They repeat their plea for him to restore them and look on them with favour.
psa-81-10: God reminds Israel that he is the one who brought them out of Egypt and invites them to open their mouths wide so he can fill them. The following verses lament that Israel refused.
psa-84-5-7: The psalm calls pilgrims blessed when their strength comes from God and their hearts are set on his house. Even a valley of weeping becomes a place of springs, as they grow stronger on the way.
psa-84-11-12: The psalmist describes God as a sun and shield who gives grace and honour. He does not hold back any good thing from those who live with integrity, and those who trust him are blessed.
psa-85-1-3: The psalm recalls how God once showed favour to his land, restored Israel, forgave their sins and set aside his anger. That memory gives hope for a fresh restoration.
psa-85-8-10: The psalmist waits to hear God speak peace to his people, if they do not return to folly. Salvation is near those who revere him, and love, faithfulness, justice and peace meet together.
psa-86-5: In his prayer, David appeals to God's character: he is good, ready to forgive and rich in love toward everyone who calls on him.
psa-86-15: David reminds himself and God of the way God described himself to Moses: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and full of love and faithfulness. He prays on that basis.
psa-87-5-6: The psalm pictures people from many nations counted as citizens of Zion. God himself keeps the register and records them as born there, a picture of the nations joining God's people.
psa-89-1-4: Ethan vows to sing for ever of the LORD's love and faithfulness. He recalls God's covenant oath to David that his dynasty and throne would last through all generations.
psa-89-33-34: Quoting God's covenant with David, the psalm says that if David's descendants sin they will be punished, but God will not withdraw his love or break his word.
psa-90-1-2: In his prayer, Moses says God has been his people's home through every generation. Before mountains or earth existed, God already was, and he will always be God.
psa-90-12: Reflecting on how short human life is, Moses asks God to teach his people to count their days, so they would live with wisdom.
psa-90-14: Moses asks God to satisfy his people early with his unfailing love, so that they can sing for joy and be glad for the rest of their days.
psa-91-1-4: The psalmist says that whoever lives close to the Most High finds shelter in his shadow. He calls God his refuge and assures the reader that God will cover and protect them.
psa-91-5-8: The psalmist encourages the believer not to fear night terrors, arrows, plagues or disaster, even if many fall nearby. It speaks of God's protection, not a promise of never suffering.
psa-91-9-13: The psalmist assures those who make the LORD their refuge of angelic protection. Satan quoted this to tempt Jesus, who refused to test God, so it is not a licence for reckless risk.
psa-91-14-16: God promises to rescue and protect the person who loves him and knows his name. He will answer them, be with them in trouble, honour them and show them his salvation.
psa-92-1-2: This Sabbath song says it is good to thank the LORD and sing praise, telling of his love each morning and his faithfulness each night.
psa-92-12-15: The psalm pictures the righteous flourishing like palm trees and cedars planted in God's house, still fruitful in old age. Their lives show that the LORD is upright and dependable.
psa-94-12-13: The psalmist says the person whom God disciplines and teaches from his law is blessed. Such teaching brings calm in hard days until the wicked are finally judged.
psa-94-14-15: While wicked rulers crush God's people, the psalmist insists the LORD will not reject or abandon them. Justice will return, and the upright will follow it.
psa-94-18-19: The psalmist remembers that when he felt his foot slipping, God's love held him up. When anxious thoughts multiplied, God's comfort brought him joy.
psa-96-11-13: The psalm calls heaven, earth, sea, fields and forests to celebrate, because the LORD is coming to judge the world. His judgment will be righteous and faithful.
psa-97-10-11: The psalmist tells those who love the LORD to hate evil, because he guards his faithful people and rescues them from the wicked. Light and joy are planted for the upright.
psa-98-1-3: The psalm calls for a new song because God has done wonders and won victory by his own power. He has made his salvation known to the nations and remembered his love for Israel.
psa-99-8: The psalm recalls that God answered Moses, Aaron and Samuel. He forgave Israel, yet still disciplined them for their wrongdoing. His mercy and holiness go together.
psa-100-5: The psalm ends its call to worship with the reason: the LORD is good, his love lasts for ever and his faithfulness continues through every generation.
psa-102-17-20: An afflicted person writes that God responds to the prayers of the destitute. This is to be recorded for future generations, so they will praise God for hearing prisoners' groans.
psa-102-25-28: The psalmist contrasts the creation, which will wear out like clothing, with God, who remains the same and whose years never end. Hebrews applies these words to Christ.
psa-103-1-5: David urges himself to praise the LORD and not forget his kindness: forgiving sin, healing, rescuing from the grave and crowning life with love and compassion.
psa-103-8-12: David says the LORD is compassionate and slow to anger. He does not punish us as our sins deserve, and he removes our wrongs as far as the east is from the west.
psa-103-13-14: David compares God's compassion to a father's tenderness toward his children. God knows how frail we are and remembers that we are only dust.
psa-103-17-18: Although human life fades like grass, David says the LORD's love lasts for ever for those who revere him, and his goodness extends to their grandchildren who keep his covenant.
psa-105-8-11: The psalm praises God for remembering his covenant for a thousand generations: the oath he made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to give Israel the land of Canaan.
psa-106-44-46: After listing Israel's repeated rebellions, the psalm notes that God still heard their cries in distress, remembered his covenant and made even their captors treat them kindly.
psa-107-1-2: The psalm opens by calling people to thank the LORD for his goodness and lasting love. Those he has rescued from their enemies should be the first to say so.
psa-107-13-16: The psalm describes prisoners who had rebelled against God. When they cried to him, he brought them out of darkness and broke their chains, so they should thank him for his love.
psa-107-19-20: The psalm pictures people made sick by their own foolish sin. When they cried to God, he sent his word, healed them and saved them from death.
psa-107-28-30: The psalm tells of sailors caught in a terrible storm. When they cried to the LORD, he calmed the sea and brought them safely to the harbour they longed for.
psa-108-12-13: Repeating words from Psalm 60, David asks God for help against the enemy, because human help is worthless. With God, his people will act bravely and win.
psa-110-1-4: David hears God invite David's Lord to sit at his right hand until his enemies are defeated, and swear that he is a priest for ever like Melchizedek. Jesus and the apostles applied this to him.
psa-111-5: The psalm praises God for providing food for those who revere him. He never forgets the covenant he has made with his people.
psa-111-9-10: The psalm praises God for rescuing his people and setting his covenant in place for ever. It concludes that revering the LORD is where wisdom begins.
psa-112-1-4: The psalm describes the blessed person who reveres God and delights in his commands. Their family and goodness endure, and even in darkness light rises for the upright.
psa-113-7-9: The psalm praises God, who lifts the poor out of the dust and seats them with princes, and gives the childless woman a home and the joy of children.
psa-115-11-13: Contrasting the LORD with lifeless idols, the psalm urges all who revere him to trust him as their help and shield. He remembers his people and will bless both great and small.
psa-116-1-9: The psalmist loves the LORD because God heard his cry when death was closing in. God rescued him from death, tears and stumbling, so he will walk before the LORD among the living.
psa-116-15: The psalmist says the death of God's faithful people is precious to the LORD. God does not treat their lives cheaply; their death matters deeply to him.
psa-118-5-6: In distress, the psalmist called on the LORD and was set free. Because God is on his side, he refuses to fear what any human could do to him.
psa-118-8-9: The psalm teaches that taking refuge in the LORD is better than relying on people, even powerful rulers. Human help has limits that God does not.
psa-118-14-17: The psalmist calls the LORD his strength, song and salvation. Joyful shouts of victory fill the tents of the righteous, and he declares that he will live to tell what God has done.
psa-118-22-24: The psalm says the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, a work of the LORD that amazes his people. Jesus applied this to himself as the rejected Messiah.
psa-119-9-11: The psalmist asks how a young person can stay pure and answers: by living according to God's word. He has stored God's word in his heart to keep from sinning.
psa-119-28: Worn down by grief, the psalmist asks God to strengthen him in line with what God has said. He looks to God's word for renewed strength.
psa-119-49: The psalmist asks God to remember the word he gave him, since it is the very thing that has given him hope.
psa-119-50: The psalmist says that in his suffering his comfort has been this: God's promise has kept him alive and renewed his strength.
psa-119-67-68: The psalmist admits he used to wander, but suffering brought him back to obeying God's word. He confesses that God is good and does good, and asks to be taught.
psa-119-71-72: The psalmist says his affliction was good for him, because it taught him God's decrees. God's instruction is now worth more to him than great wealth.
psa-119-76: The psalmist asks that God's unfailing love would comfort him, just as God has promised his servant.
psa-119-105: The psalmist compares God's word to a lamp for his feet and a light for his path. It shows him the next step and keeps him from stumbling in the dark.
psa-119-114: The psalmist calls God his hiding place and shield. His hope rests on God's word.
psa-119-116: The psalmist asks God to sustain him according to his promise so that he may live, and not let his hope end in disappointment.
psa-119-165: The psalmist observes that those who love God's law have deep peace, and nothing makes them stumble.
psa-120-1: The first of the pilgrim songs begins with the writer's experience: when he was in distress he called to the LORD, and God answered him.
psa-121-1-4: In a pilgrim song, the writer looks toward the hills and asks where help will come from. He answers that it comes from the LORD, the Creator, who never sleeps, so he depends on God, not earthly protection.
psa-121-5-8: The psalm assures the traveller that the LORD is their keeper and shade, guarding them day and night. He will watch over their whole life, their going out and coming in, for ever.
psa-124-6-8: Israel praises the LORD for not letting their enemies devour them. They escaped like a bird from a broken trap, because their help is in the name of the Maker of heaven and earth.
psa-125-1-2: The psalm says those who trust the LORD are as secure as Mount Zion, which cannot be moved. As mountains surround Jerusalem, God surrounds his people for ever.
psa-126-5-6: Remembering a past restoration, the returning exiles pray that those who sow with tears will reap with songs of joy. They hope present sorrow will turn into a harvest of gladness.
psa-127-1-2: This pilgrim song teaches that building and guarding are useless unless the LORD is behind them. Anxious overwork achieves nothing, for God gives rest to those he loves.
psa-127-3-5: The psalm describes children as a gift and reward from the LORD. Like arrows in a warrior's hand, many children were seen as strength and honour for a family.
psa-128-1-4: The psalm describes the blessing on a household that reveres God: enjoying the fruit of their work, a fruitful marriage and children around the table. It is a picture of God's favour, not a formula.
psa-130-1-2: From the depths of distress, the psalmist cries out and begs God to listen closely to his plea for mercy.
psa-130-3-5: The psalmist admits no one could stand if God kept a record of sins, yet God forgives, so people revere him. He waits for the LORD and puts his hope in his word.
psa-130-7-8: The psalmist calls Israel to hope in the LORD, because with him is unfailing love and full redemption. He will rescue his people from all their sins.
psa-131-1-3: David says he is not proud or chasing things too great for him. He has calmed himself like a weaned child resting with its mother, and urges Israel to hope in the LORD.
psa-132-11-12: The psalm recalls God's sworn promise that David's descendants would sit on his throne, and that their line would continue as long as they kept God's covenant.
psa-132-13-16: The psalm says God chose Zion as his home for ever. He promised to bless its food supply, satisfy its poor, clothe its priests with salvation and fill its faithful with joy.
psa-133-1-3: David praises how good it is when God's people live together in unity. He compares it to fragrant anointing oil and refreshing dew, where the LORD gives his blessing of life.
psa-135-13-14: The psalm praises God's name as lasting through all generations. He will defend his people and have compassion on his servants, unlike idols that cannot act.
psa-136-1-3: This responsive psalm calls worshippers to thank the LORD, the God of gods and Lord of lords. Each line answers with the refrain that his love endures for ever.
psa-138-1-3: David thanks God wholeheartedly for his love and faithfulness. When David called, God answered and made him bold with fresh strength.
psa-138-7-8: David is confident that even in the middle of trouble God will keep him alive and save him. The LORD will complete his purpose for David, because his love lasts for ever.
psa-139-1-6: David marvels that God knows him completely: his actions, thoughts and words before he speaks. Such knowledge is too wonderful for him to grasp.
psa-139-7-12: David realises there is nowhere he could escape from God's presence, not in heaven, the grave or the farthest sea. Even darkness is not dark to God.
psa-139-13-16: David praises God for forming him in his mother's womb with wonderful care. Before he was born, God saw him and knew all the days planned for him.
psa-139-23-24: David asks God to search his heart and test his anxious thoughts, to show him anything offensive in him and to lead him in the way that lasts for ever.
psa-140-12-13: Facing violent men, David is sure the LORD will defend the poor and bring justice to the needy. The righteous will give thanks and live in God's presence.
psa-141-1-2: David asks God to come quickly and hear him. He wants his prayer to rise before God like incense, and his raised hands to be like the evening sacrifice.
psa-142-1-5: Hiding in a cave with no one to care for him, David pours out his complaint to God. He declares that God is his refuge and all he has in this life.
psa-143-8-10: David asks to hear of God's love each morning, to be shown the way he should go and rescued from enemies. He asks God's good Spirit to teach him to do God's will.
psa-144-1-2: David, a warrior king, praises God as his rock, who trained him for battle. God is his love, fortress, stronghold, deliverer and shield.
psa-144-15: After describing a nation at peace and prospering, David concludes that the people whose God is the LORD are truly blessed.
psa-145-8-9: David praises the LORD as gracious, compassionate, slow to anger and rich in love. He is good to everyone and kind to all he has made.
psa-145-13-16: David praises God's everlasting kingdom and his faithfulness to every promise. He lifts those who fall and feeds every living thing at the right time.
psa-145-17-20: David says God is just and kind in everything he does. He is near to all who call on him sincerely, hears their cry and protects those who love him, while the wicked face judgment.
psa-146-5-9: After warning against trusting rulers, the psalm calls happy those whose help is the God of Jacob. The Creator keeps faith, feeds the hungry, frees prisoners and cares for foreigners, orphans and widows.
psa-147-3: The psalm praises God, who rebuilds Jerusalem and gathers its exiles, as the one who heals those whose hearts are broken and bandages their wounds.
psa-147-11: The psalm says God is not impressed by the strength of horses or soldiers. What delights him is people who revere him and rely on his unfailing love.
psa-149-4: The psalm calls Israel to celebrate because the LORD delights in his people and honours the humble by saving them.
pro-1-7: Proverbs opens with its key idea: reverence for the LORD is the starting point of true knowledge. Only fools reject wisdom and correction.
pro-1-23: Wisdom, pictured as a woman calling in the streets, urges the careless to respond to her warning. If they turn, she will pour out her thoughts and make her teaching known to them.
pro-1-33: Ending her warning to those who ignore her, Wisdom says that whoever listens to her will live in safety and be free from the dread of disaster.
pro-2-6-8: A father tells his son that wisdom is God's gift. The LORD stores up sound judgment for the upright, shields those with integrity and guards the way of his faithful people.
pro-3-1-2: A father urges his son not to forget his teaching but keep it in his heart. Living this way generally brings long life and peace, though Proverbs offers principles rather than guarantees.
pro-3-5-6: A father urges his son to rely fully on God rather than his own judgment, and to honour God in every part of life. It is a wisdom principle: God guides those who trust him, but no easy path is guaranteed.
pro-3-7-8: The father warns his son against thinking himself wise. Revering the LORD and turning from evil brings a healthy, whole life, as a general rule of wisdom.
pro-3-9-10: The father tells his son to honour the LORD with the first and best of his produce. In Israel's farming world this was linked with full barns, describing God's usual blessing, not a payment scheme.
pro-3-11-12: The father urges his son not to resent the LORD's correction, because God disciplines those he loves, as a father corrects a son he delights in. Hebrews 12 quotes this.
pro-3-13-18: The father says the person who finds wisdom is blessed, since she is worth more than silver, gold or jewels. Wisdom brings long life, honour, pleasant ways and peace, like a tree of life.
pro-3-21-26: The father tells his son to hold on to sound judgment, which brings life and a secure walk. He can sleep without fear, because the LORD will be his confidence and keep him from traps.
pro-4-5-7: A father urges his son to make getting wisdom his priority, whatever it costs. If he loves and holds on to wisdom, it will protect and guard him.
pro-4-18: The father compares the life of the righteous to the dawn, which grows brighter and brighter until full day. In contrast, the way of the wicked is deep darkness.
pro-4-20-22: A father asks his son to pay close attention to his words and keep them in his heart, because wise teaching brings life and wholeness to those who take hold of it.
pro-6-20-23: The father urges his son to keep his parents' teaching close. It will guide him when he walks, guard him when he sleeps and speak to him when he wakes, like a lamp.
pro-8-17: Wisdom, speaking as a person, says she loves those who love her, and those who look for her earnestly will find her. Seeking wisdom is never wasted effort.
pro-8-32-35: Wisdom calls her listeners to heed her and keep her ways, waiting at her door daily. Whoever finds her finds life and receives favour from the LORD.
pro-9-10-11: Proverbs repeats that reverence for the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowing the Holy One is real understanding. Wisdom says she adds years to life.
pro-10-3: This proverb observes that the LORD does not let the righteous starve but frustrates the cravings of the wicked. It describes God's general care, not a promise against every hardship.
pro-10-12: This proverb contrasts hatred, which stirs up conflict, with love, which covers over offences instead of exposing them. Peter quotes this in urging Christians to love one another.
pro-10-22: Solomon observes that the LORD's blessing makes people rich without adding the sorrow that often comes with wealth gained by toil and greed.
pro-11-2: This proverb warns that pride leads to disgrace, while humility goes hand in hand with wisdom.
pro-11-24-25: Solomon notes a paradox: generous people often end up with more, while stingy people end up in need. Those who refresh others will themselves be refreshed.
pro-12-25: This proverb observes that anxiety weighs a person down, but a kind and encouraging word can lift their heart.
pro-13-12: Solomon observes that hope that keeps being delayed makes a person sick at heart, but a longing finally fulfilled brings new life, like a tree of life.
pro-14-26-27: This proverb says that revering the LORD gives a person strong security and a refuge for their children. It is like a fountain of life that turns people away from deadly traps.
pro-15-1: This proverb teaches that a gentle reply can calm anger, while harsh words stir it up. How we answer often decides whether conflict grows.
pro-15-13: Solomon observes that a happy heart shows on the face, while heartache crushes the spirit. Our inner state affects our whole life.
pro-15-29: This proverb says the LORD keeps his distance from the wicked but listens to the prayers of those who live rightly.
pro-16-3: This proverb advises entrusting all our work to the LORD. Plans made in dependence on God tend to stand, though Proverbs also says God decides the final outcome.
pro-16-7: Solomon observes that when a person's life pleases the LORD, God can even turn enemies toward peace with them. It is a general pattern, not a promise of no opposition.
pro-16-9: This proverb notes that people make their plans, but it is the LORD who determines their steps. Planning is wise, but God has the final say.
pro-18-10: This proverb pictures the LORD's name as a strong tower. The righteous run to him and are safe, in contrast to the rich, who trust in their wealth.
pro-18-14: Solomon observes that a healthy spirit can carry a person through illness, but a crushed spirit is almost impossible to bear.
pro-18-24: This proverb warns that having many casual companions can lead to ruin, but a true friend can be more loyal than a brother.
pro-19-17: Solomon teaches that kindness to the poor is like lending to the LORD himself, and God will repay what was given.
pro-19-21: This proverb observes that people may have many plans, but it is the LORD's purpose that finally stands.
pro-19-23: Solomon says that revering the LORD leads to life, so a person can rest content and untouched by harm. It describes the general fruit of reverence, not immunity from trouble.
pro-20-22: This proverb warns against taking revenge. Instead, wait for the LORD, and he will bring deliverance. Paul echoes this in Romans 12.
pro-21-5: Solomon contrasts careful, diligent planning, which tends to bring gain, with hasty shortcuts, which usually lead to poverty.
pro-21-30-31: This proverb says no human wisdom or plan can succeed against the LORD. People prepare horses for battle, but victory belongs to God.
pro-22-4: Solomon observes that humility and reverence for the LORD tend to bring riches, honour and life. This is the normal pattern of wisdom, not a promise of wealth.
pro-22-6: This proverb encourages parents to train a child in the way they should go, since early training usually shapes the whole of life. It is a principle, not a promise that every child will follow.
pro-24-13-14: Just as honey is sweet and good, the writer tells his son, wisdom is good for the soul. If he finds it, he will have a future, and his hope will not be cut off.
pro-24-16: This proverb says the righteous may fall many times and still get up again, while the wicked are brought down by disaster. It warns those who plot against the godly.
pro-28-13: This proverb teaches that hiding our sins leads nowhere good, but confessing and turning away from them brings mercy.
pro-29-25: Solomon warns that fear of what people think becomes a trap, but whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe.
pro-30-5: Agur, a wisdom teacher, says every word of God is pure and proven true. God shields those who take refuge in him, so nothing should be added to his words.
ecc-3-11: The Teacher reflects that God makes everything beautiful in its proper time. He has put a sense of eternity in human hearts, yet people cannot grasp all that God is doing.
ecc-3-14: The Teacher concludes that what God does lasts for ever; nothing can be added or taken away. God acts this way so people will stand in awe of him.
ecc-5-19-20: The Teacher says the ability to enjoy wealth, work and life is itself a gift from God. Those given that joy are kept so busy with gladness that they do not brood over life's brevity.
ecc-12-13-14: The Teacher sums up the whole book: revere God and keep his commands, because this is everyone's duty. God will judge every deed, including hidden ones, good or evil.
isa-1-18: After accusing Judah of corruption, God invites them to settle the matter with him. Sins stained deep red can be washed white as snow, if they are willing to obey.
isa-2-2-4: Isaiah foresees a day when the nations stream to the LORD's temple to learn his ways. God will settle disputes, and people will turn weapons into farming tools and stop training for war.
isa-4-5-6: Isaiah promised that after cleansing Jerusalem, God would cover Zion with cloud by day and fire by night, as in the exodus. His glory would be a shelter from heat and storm.
isa-6-6-7: In Isaiah's vision, after he confessed his unclean lips, a seraph touched his mouth with a burning coal from the altar and declared his guilt removed and his sin forgiven.
isa-7-14: Isaiah told faithless King Ahaz that God would give a sign: a young woman would bear a son named Immanuel, "God with us". Matthew sees the full meaning in Jesus' birth to the virgin Mary.
isa-9-2: Isaiah foretold that people living in darkness and under the shadow of death would see a great light. Matthew applies this to Jesus' ministry in Galilee.
isa-9-6-7: Isaiah foretold the birth of a royal child with names like Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God and Prince of Peace. His just reign on David's throne would grow without end; Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus.
isa-10-20-21: Isaiah foretold that after Assyria's attack, a remnant of Israel would stop relying on the power that struck them and truly rely on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, returning to the mighty God.
isa-11-1-5: Isaiah foretold that a new shoot would grow from the stump of Jesse's family. The LORD's Spirit would rest on this king, who would judge the poor fairly and rule with righteousness. Christians see Jesus here.
isa-11-6-9: Isaiah pictures the Messiah's reign as a world where wolves live with lambs and children play safely near snakes. No harm will be done, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD.
isa-12-1-2: Isaiah gives the rescued people a song for that future day: God's anger has turned to comfort. They will trust him without fear, because the LORD is their strength, song and salvation.
isa-12-3: Isaiah tells the restored people that they will joyfully draw water from the wells of salvation, an image of drinking deeply from God's rescue as from a spring.
isa-14-1-2: Isaiah promised that after Babylon fell, the LORD would again show compassion on Israel, choose them, settle them in their land and draw foreigners to join them.
isa-25-6-8: Isaiah foresees God preparing a rich feast for all peoples on his mountain. He will remove the shroud of death, swallow up death for ever and wipe away every tear. Paul and Revelation echo this.
isa-26-3-4: In a song for the day of salvation, God's people declare that he keeps in perfect peace those whose minds rest on him because they trust him. The LORD is a rock that lasts for ever.
isa-26-12: Judah's song tells the LORD that he will establish peace for them, since everything they have accomplished has really been his work.
