jhn-15-4-5: Jesus urges his disciples to stay joined to him, as a branch can only bear fruit while attached to the vine. Whoever remains in him bears much fruit, but apart from him they can do nothing.
jhn-15-7-8: Jesus promises that if his disciples remain in him and his words shape them, they can ask whatever they wish and it will be done. Their fruitfulness brings glory to the Father.
jhn-15-9-11: Jesus says he loves his disciples as the Father loves him, and calls them to stay in his love by keeping his commands. He tells them this so his joy may be in them and their joy complete.
jhn-15-12-13: Jesus commands his disciples to love each other as he has loved them. The greatest love is to lay down one's life for friends, as he was about to do.
jhn-15-15-16: Jesus calls his disciples friends, not servants, because he has shared with them everything from the Father. He chose them to bear lasting fruit, so the Father will give what they ask in his name.
jhn-15-26: Jesus promised his disciples that he would send the Helper, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father. The Spirit would testify about Jesus, and so would they.
jhn-16-7: Jesus told his grieving disciples that his leaving was for their good, because unless he went away the Helper would not come. When he went, he would send the Spirit to them.
jhn-16-13-14: Jesus promised his disciples that the Spirit of truth would guide them into all truth and tell them what was to come. The Spirit would bring glory to Jesus by making him known.
jhn-16-20-22: Jesus promises his disciples that their grief will turn to joy, like a mother's after childbirth. They would weep while the world rejoiced, but when they saw him again no one could take that joy away.
jhn-16-23-24: Jesus promises that after his resurrection the Father will give whatever his disciples ask in Jesus' name. He urges them to ask and receive, so that their joy may be complete.
jhn-16-27: Jesus assures his disciples that the Father himself loves them, because they have loved Jesus and believed that he came from God. They can approach the Father directly.
jhn-16-33: Jesus tells his disciples plainly that they will have trouble in this world. But they can have peace in him and take courage, because he has overcome the world.
jhn-17-3: In his prayer before his arrest, Jesus defines eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. It is a relationship, not merely endless time.
jhn-17-11: Jesus prays for his disciples, who will remain in the world after he leaves. He asks the Holy Father to protect them by his name, so that they may be one as the Father and Son are one.
jhn-17-15-17: Jesus does not ask the Father to take his disciples out of the world but to protect them from the evil one. He asks God to make them holy through the truth of his word.
jhn-17-20-23: Jesus prays for all who will believe through the apostles' message, asking that they be one as he and the Father are one. Their unity will show the world that God sent him and loves them.
jhn-17-24: Jesus asks the Father that those given to him may be with him where he is and see the glory the Father gave him, because the Father loved him before the world began.
jhn-17-26: Jesus ends his prayer saying he has made the Father known and will continue to do so, so that the Father's love for him may be in his followers, and he himself in them.
jhn-20-19-21: On the evening of his resurrection, Jesus came to his fearful disciples behind locked doors and said, "Peace be with you." He showed them his wounds and sent them as the Father had sent him.
jhn-20-22-23: The risen Jesus breathed on his disciples and told them to receive the Holy Spirit. He gave them authority to declare sins forgiven, or not, as they proclaimed his message.
jhn-20-27-29: Jesus invited doubting Thomas to touch his wounds, and Thomas confessed him as "my Lord and my God". Jesus then blessed all who would believe without having seen him.
jhn-20-31: John explains why he wrote his Gospel: so readers may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.
act-1-8: Before returning to heaven, Jesus promised the apostles that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came on them. They would be his witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.
act-2-17-18: At Pentecost Peter explained that the disciples were not drunk. Joel's prophecy was being fulfilled: in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on all kinds of people, sons and daughters, young and old.
act-2-21: Concluding his quotation of Joel, Peter told the crowd that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, and then showed that this Lord is Jesus.
act-2-38-39: When the crowd asked what to do, Peter told them to repent and be baptised in Jesus' name for forgiveness, and they would receive the Holy Spirit. This promise reaches their children and all whom God calls.
act-3-19-21: After healing a lame man, Peter urged the crowd to repent and turn to God so their sins would be wiped out. Times of refreshing would come, and God would send Jesus again at the final restoration.
act-4-12: On trial before the council, Peter declared that salvation is found in no one else but Jesus. No other name under heaven has been given by which people must be saved.
act-10-34-35: In the home of the Roman officer Cornelius, Peter realised that God does not show favouritism. He accepts people from every nation who revere him and do what is right.
act-10-43: Peter told Cornelius and his household that all the prophets testify about Jesus: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.
act-13-38-39: Preaching in a synagogue, Paul announced that forgiveness of sins is offered through Jesus. Everyone who believes is set right with God in every way the law of Moses could never achieve.
act-16-31: When the terrified jailer asked what he must do to be saved, Paul and Silas told him to believe in the Lord Jesus, and he and his household would be saved. His family heard and believed too.
act-18-9-10: In a night vision at Corinth, the Lord told Paul not to be afraid but to keep speaking. He promised that no one would harm him there, because many people in the city belonged to him.
act-26-17-18: Paul tells King Agrippa how Jesus sent him to the Gentiles to open their eyes, turning them from darkness to light and from Satan to God, so they could receive forgiveness and a place among God's people.
rom-1-16-17: Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew and Gentile alike. It reveals a righteousness from God received by faith from start to finish.
rom-3-21-24: Paul explains that God has now revealed a way to be right with him apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ. Everyone has sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by his grace.
rom-3-25-26: Paul explains that God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, received through faith. This shows God is just: he does not ignore sin, yet he justifies those who trust in Jesus.
rom-4-5: Paul explains, using Abraham, that God counts as righteous the person who trusts him rather than relying on their own works, the God who justifies the ungodly.
rom-4-7-8: Paul quotes David's psalm to show that being right with God is a gift: blessed are those whose wrongs are forgiven and whose sins the Lord will never count against them.
rom-4-16-17: Paul explains that God's promise to Abraham comes by faith and grace, so it is guaranteed to all his spiritual children, not only those under the law. Abraham trusted the God who gives life to the dead.
rom-4-20-22: Paul says Abraham did not waver in unbelief at God's promise of a son, but grew strong in faith, fully convinced God could do what he had promised. That faith was credited to him as righteousness.
rom-5-1-2: Paul tells believers that, since they are made right with God through faith, they now have peace with him through Jesus. They stand in his grace and rejoice in the hope of sharing God's glory.
rom-5-3-5: Paul tells believers they can even rejoice in suffering, because it produces endurance, character and hope. This hope will not disappoint them, because God has poured his love into their hearts by the Spirit.
rom-5-6-8: Paul points out that people rarely die even for a good person. But God showed his love for us in this: Christ died for us while we were still powerless sinners.
rom-5-9-11: Paul reasons that if Christ's death reconciled us to God while we were enemies, then now that we are made right with him, we will surely be saved from judgment through his risen life.
rom-5-17: Paul contrasts Adam and Christ: through one man's sin death ruled. Far more, those who receive God's abundant grace and gift of righteousness will reign in life through Jesus Christ.
rom-5-20-21: Paul explains that the law made sin more visible, but where sin increased, God's grace increased even more. Grace now reigns, bringing eternal life through Jesus Christ.
rom-6-4-5: Paul tells believers that through baptism they were united with Christ in his death and burial. As Christ was raised, they too can now live a new life, and they will share his resurrection.
rom-6-14: Paul assures believers that sin will no longer be their master, because they are not under the law but under grace. This is a reason to resist sin, not permission to keep sinning.
rom-6-23: Paul contrasts two outcomes: sin pays its wage, which is death, but God gives a free gift, eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Life cannot be earned, only received.
rom-8-1-2: Paul declares that there is now no condemnation for those who belong to Christ Jesus. Through Christ, the Spirit who gives life has set them free from the power of sin and death.
rom-8-6: Paul contrasts two mindsets: a mind governed by sinful human nature leads to death, but a mind governed by the Spirit brings life and peace.
rom-8-9-11: Paul tells believers that God's Spirit lives in them, marking them as Christ's. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to their mortal bodies.
rom-8-14-16: Paul says that those led by God's Spirit are God's children. They have not received a spirit of fearful slavery but of adoption, so they cry "Abba, Father", and the Spirit confirms they belong to God.
rom-8-17: Paul explains that as God's children, believers are also his heirs, sharing Christ's inheritance. If they share in his sufferings, they will also share in his glory.
rom-8-18: Paul weighs present suffering against future glory and concludes that today's sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory God will reveal in his people.
rom-8-26-27: Paul assures believers that when they are weak and do not know what to pray, the Spirit himself prays for them with groans beyond words. God, who searches hearts, knows the Spirit's mind.
rom-8-28: Paul encourages suffering Christians. He does not call every event good. Rather, God works through all circumstances, hardship included, for the ultimate good of those who love him: growth in faith and final salvation.
rom-8-29-30: Paul explains God's purpose: those he foreknew he planned to shape into the likeness of his Son. He called them, made them right with him, and will surely bring them to glory.
rom-8-31-32: Paul asks who can stand against us if God is for us. Since God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, he will surely give us everything we need with him.
rom-8-33-34: Paul asks who could accuse God's chosen people, since God himself declares them righteous. No one can condemn them, because Christ died, rose and now pleads for them at God's right hand.
rom-8-35-37: Paul lists hardships like persecution, hunger and the sword and asks whether any can separate us from Christ's love. Even when suffering, believers are more than conquerors through him who loved them.
rom-8-38-39: Paul declares his conviction that nothing in life or death, no spiritual power, nothing present or future, nor anything else in creation can separate believers from God's love in Christ Jesus.
rom-10-9-11: Paul explains that whoever openly confesses Jesus as Lord and truly believes God raised him from the dead will be saved. Quoting Isaiah, he adds that no one who trusts in him will be put to shame.
rom-10-12-13: Paul stresses that there is no difference between Jew and Gentile: the same Lord richly blesses all who call on him. Quoting Joel, he says everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved.
rom-11-29: Speaking of Israel's future, Paul says that God never takes back his gifts or his call. His commitments to his people are irrevocable.
rom-12-1-2: In view of God's mercy, Paul urges believers to offer their whole lives to God as living sacrifices. Instead of copying the world's ways, they should be transformed by a renewed mind, so they can discern God's will.
rom-12-12: Among his practical instructions for Christian living, Paul urges believers to be joyful in hope, patient when trouble comes and faithful in prayer.
rom-12-19: Paul tells believers not to take revenge but to leave room for God's justice. Quoting Deuteronomy, he reminds them that God says vengeance belongs to him and he will repay.
rom-15-4: Paul says the Old Testament Scriptures were written to teach us, so that through the endurance and encouragement they give, we might have hope.
rom-15-13: Paul prays a blessing over believers: that the God of hope would fill them with joy and peace as they trust him, so they overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
1co-1-8-9: Despite the Corinthians' many problems, Paul tells them that God will keep them strong to the end, so they will be blameless when Christ returns. God, who called them into fellowship with his Son, is faithful.
1co-1-18: Paul says the message of the cross seems foolish to those who are perishing, but to those being saved it is the very power of God.
1co-1-27-29: Paul reminds the Corinthians that few of them were influential. God chose what the world counts foolish, weak and lowly to shame the proud, so that no one can boast before him.
1co-2-9-10: Paul quotes Scripture: no eye has seen and no mind imagined what God has prepared for those who love him. But God has revealed it to believers by his Spirit, who searches even God's depths.
1co-2-12: Paul tells believers they have not received the world's way of thinking but God's own Spirit, so they can understand what God has freely given them.
1co-3-16-17: Paul reminds the divided Corinthian church that together they are God's temple, where his Spirit lives. Anyone who destroys this temple through division will face God's judgment, because it is holy.
1co-6-14: Arguing that the body matters to God, Paul says that God raised the Lord Jesus and will raise believers too by his power.
1co-6-19-20: Warning against sexual immorality, Paul reminds believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit. They do not belong to themselves, since they were bought at a price, so they should honour God with their bodies.
1co-10-13: Paul tells believers that every temptation they face is common to people. God is faithful and will not let them be tested beyond what they can bear, but will provide a way out so they can endure.
1co-12-4-7: Paul explains that there are many kinds of spiritual gifts, service and work, but the same Spirit, Lord and God behind them all. Each believer is given a gift for the good of everyone.
1co-13-4-8: Paul describes real love for a church divided by pride: it is patient and kind, not jealous, boastful or rude. It keeps no record of wrongs, always protects and hopes, and never fails.
1co-13-12-13: Paul says that now we see God only dimly, like a reflection in an old mirror, but one day we will see face to face and know fully. Faith, hope and love last, and love is the greatest.
1co-15-3-4: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the core of the gospel he passed on to them: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised on the third day, as the Scriptures foretold.
1co-15-20-22: Paul declares that Christ has truly risen, the first of a great harvest. As death came to all through Adam, so all who belong to Christ will be made alive through him.
1co-15-51-52: Paul reveals a mystery: not all believers will die, but all will be changed in an instant at the last trumpet. The dead will rise with imperishable bodies, and the living will be transformed.
1co-15-54-57: Paul says that when our mortal bodies are made immortal, death will be swallowed up in victory and lose its sting. He thanks God, who gives that victory through Jesus Christ.
1co-15-58: After teaching on the resurrection, Paul urges believers to stand firm and keep giving themselves fully to the Lord's work. Because Christ has risen, nothing they do for him is wasted.
1co-16-13-14: In his closing words, Paul tells the Corinthians to stay alert, hold firmly to the faith and be brave and strong, while making sure everything they do is done in love.
2co-1-3-4: Paul praises God as the merciful Father who comforts his people in every trouble. That comfort is meant to be passed on, so they can comfort others who are suffering.
2co-1-5: Paul says that as he shares abundantly in Christ's sufferings, he also receives abundant comfort through Christ. The comfort keeps pace with the hardship.
2co-1-20: Defending his reliability, Paul says that every promise God has made finds its "Yes" in Christ, who fulfils them. That is why believers say "Amen" through him, to God's glory.
2co-1-21-22: Paul says it is God who makes believers stand firm in Christ. He has marked them as his own and given his Spirit as a deposit guaranteeing what is still to come.
2co-3-17-18: Paul explains that where the Lord's Spirit is, there is freedom. As believers look at the Lord's glory without a veil, the Spirit gradually changes them into his likeness.
2co-4-6: Paul compares conversion to creation: the God who first commanded light to shine in darkness has shone into believers' hearts, showing them his glory in the face of Jesus Christ.
2co-4-7-9: Paul describes the gospel as treasure in fragile clay jars, so the power is clearly God's. He and his co-workers are hard pressed, confused and persecuted, yet never crushed, abandoned or destroyed.
2co-4-16-18: Paul says he does not lose heart: though his body is wearing out, his inner life is renewed daily. Present troubles are brief compared with the lasting glory they are producing, so he looks to what is unseen.
2co-5-1: Paul compares the body to a tent that will be taken down at death. Believers know that God has a permanent, heavenly dwelling waiting for them, not built by human hands.
2co-5-5: Paul says that God himself has prepared believers for this future of resurrection life and has given them the Spirit as a deposit guaranteeing it.
2co-5-7: Explaining why he is confident even while away from the Lord, Paul says believers live by trusting God, not by what they can see.
2co-5-17: Paul declares that anyone united with Christ is a new creation. The old way of life is gone, and something entirely new has begun.
2co-5-18-19: Paul explains that God took the initiative to reconcile people to himself through Christ, no longer counting their sins against them. He has now given believers the task of sharing that message.
2co-5-21: Paul explains the great exchange: God made the sinless Christ to bear sin on our behalf, so that in union with him we might be made right with God.
2co-6-2: Paul quotes Isaiah's words about God hearing and helping at the right time. He then urges the Corinthians not to delay, because now is the time God offers salvation.
2co-6-16-18: Paul tells believers they are the temple of the living God, so they must not mix with idolatry. He weaves together Old Testament promises that God will live among them and be their Father.
2co-7-6: Paul recalls being worn out and anxious in Macedonia. God, who comforts the downcast, encouraged him by bringing Titus with good news from Corinth.
2co-9-6-8: Urging generosity for poor believers, Paul says that those who give generously will reap generously. God loves a cheerful giver and can provide all they need so they can keep doing good; it is not a formula for getting rich.
2co-9-10-11: Paul prays that God, who gives seed to the farmer and bread to eat, will supply and increase their resources for giving. Their generosity will lead many to thank God.
2co-12-9-10: Paul tells how he begged God to remove a painful "thorn in the flesh", but the Lord answered that his grace was enough, because his power works best in weakness. So Paul learned to accept his weaknesses.
2co-13-11: In his final appeal, Paul urges the Corinthians to rejoice, mend their ways, encourage each other, agree and live in peace. Then the God of love and peace will be with them.
2co-13-14: Paul closes the letter with a blessing naming Father, Son and Spirit: the grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit with them all.
gal-2-20: Paul says his old self died with Christ on the cross, and now Christ lives in him. He lives his present life by trusting the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him.
gal-3-13-14: Paul explains that Christ freed us from the law's curse by taking it on himself on the cross. This opened the blessing promised to Abraham to the Gentiles, so all may receive the Spirit by faith.
gal-3-26-29: Paul tells believers they are all God's children through faith in Christ. Divisions of race, status and sex no longer separate them in Christ, and they are Abraham's heirs by God's promise.
gal-4-4-7: Paul says that at the right time God sent his Son, born under the law, to free people and adopt them as children. God sent his Spirit into their hearts crying "Abba, Father", so they are heirs, not slaves.
gal-5-1: Paul urges the Galatians to hold on to the freedom Christ won for them, and not to return to the slavery of trying to earn God's favour through the law.
gal-5-13-14: Paul reminds believers they were called to freedom, but not to use it as an excuse for selfishness. Instead they should serve each other in love, which fulfils the whole law.
gal-5-16-18: Paul tells believers to live by the Spirit, so they will not follow the desires of their sinful nature. These two are in conflict, but those led by the Spirit are not under the law.
gal-5-22-23: Paul lists the qualities the Holy Spirit grows in believers: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. No law forbids such things.
gal-6-2: Paul tells believers to help carry one another's heavy loads, especially those struggling with sin. In doing so they fulfil Christ's law of love.
gal-6-7-9: Paul warns that God cannot be fooled: people reap what they sow. Living for selfish desires leads to ruin, but living by the Spirit leads to eternal life, so believers should not grow tired of doing good.
eph-1-3-6: Paul praises God for blessing believers with every spiritual blessing in Christ. Before creation God chose them to be holy and, out of love, planned to adopt them as his children through Jesus.
eph-1-7-8: Paul says that in Christ believers are set free through his blood and their sins are forgiven, because God has poured out his rich grace on them with wisdom and understanding.
eph-1-13-14: Paul tells believers that when they heard and believed the gospel, God marked them with the promised Holy Spirit. The Spirit is a guarantee of their future inheritance as God's own people.
eph-2-4-7: Paul explains that although we were spiritually dead in sin, God, rich in mercy and love, made us alive with Christ. He raised us with him to show the riches of his kindness for ages to come.
eph-2-8-10: Paul explains that salvation is God's gift, received through faith and not earned by effort, so no one can boast. Believers are God's handiwork, created in Christ to do the good works he has prepared.
eph-2-13-14: Paul tells Gentile believers that they were once far from God and his people, but Christ's blood has brought them near. Christ himself is their peace, breaking down the wall that divided Jews and Gentiles.
eph-2-18-19: Paul says that through Christ both Jews and Gentiles can approach the Father by the one Spirit. Gentile believers are no longer outsiders but full citizens and members of God's family.
eph-2-20-22: Paul pictures the church as a building founded on the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. Believers are being joined together into a holy temple where God lives by his Spirit.
eph-3-12: Paul says that through faith in Christ, believers can come to God freely and confidently, without fear.
eph-3-16-19: Paul prays that God would strengthen believers inwardly by his Spirit, so Christ may live in their hearts. Rooted in love, they may grasp how vast Christ's love is and be filled with God's fullness.
eph-3-20-21: Paul closes his prayer by praising God, who is able to do far more than we ask or imagine by his power at work in us. He gives God glory in the church and in Christ for ever.
eph-4-4-6: Urging unity, Paul reminds believers of what they share: one body, one Spirit and one hope, one Lord, faith and baptism, and one God and Father over all.
eph-4-22-24: Paul tells believers to put off their old self, corrupted by deceitful desires, and to be renewed in their thinking. They should put on the new self, created to be like God in righteousness and holiness.
eph-4-26-27: Paul allows that anger can be right but warns not to let it lead to sin. Settle it quickly, before the day ends, so the devil gets no opportunity.
eph-4-32: Paul urges believers to be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other in the same way God forgave them in Christ.
eph-5-1-2: Paul tells believers to imitate God as his dearly loved children. They should live a life of love, following Christ, who loved them and gave himself as a sacrifice to God.
eph-5-8-9: Paul reminds believers that they once belonged to darkness, but now they are light because of the Lord. They should live as children of light, showing goodness, righteousness and truth.
eph-5-14: Paul quotes what seems to be an early Christian saying that calls sleepers to wake up and rise from the dead. When they do, Christ will shine his light on them.
eph-6-10-11: In his closing section, Paul urges believers to find their strength in the Lord's mighty power. They should put on all of God's armour so they can stand firm against the devil's schemes.
eph-6-13: Paul repeats his call to put on God's full armour, so that when evil attacks, believers can resist and, after doing everything, still be standing.
eph-6-16-17: Paul tells believers to take up faith as a shield to put out the evil one's flaming arrows. They should also wear salvation as a helmet and use God's word, the Spirit's sword.
php-1-6: Paul tells the Philippians he is confident that God, who started a good work in them, will keep at it until it is finished on the day Christ returns.
php-1-21: Facing possible execution in prison, Paul says that for him living means serving Christ, and dying means being with him, which is even better.
php-2-13: Paul urges the Philippians to work out their salvation, explaining that God himself is at work in them, giving them both the desire and the power to do what pleases him.
php-3-20-21: Paul reminds believers that their true citizenship is in heaven, and they eagerly wait for the Lord Jesus to come from there. He will transform their weak bodies to be like his glorious body.
php-4-4-5: Paul urges the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord at all times and to let everyone see their gentleness, because the Lord is near.
php-4-6-7: Paul tells believers not to be anxious but to bring every need to God in prayer, with thanks. Then God's peace, deeper than human understanding, will guard their hearts and minds in Christ.
php-4-8-9: Paul urges believers to fill their minds with whatever is true, honourable, right, pure, lovely and admirable, and to practise what they learned from him. Then the God of peace will be with them.
php-4-11-13: Writing from prison and thanking the Philippians for their gift, Paul says he has learned contentment with plenty or little. "I can do all things" means facing any circumstance through Christ's strength, not unlimited achievement.
php-4-19: Paul assures the generous Philippians, who had given to support him, that his God will meet all their needs from his glorious riches in Christ Jesus. It concerns needs, not every wish.
col-1-11-12: Paul prays that believers would be strengthened by God's glorious power so they can endure patiently and joyfully, thanking the Father who has qualified them to share his people's inheritance in light.
col-1-13-14: Paul tells believers that God has rescued them from the power of darkness and brought them into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom they are set free and forgiven.
col-1-19-20: Paul explains that God's full nature was pleased to live in Christ. Through him God chose to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through Jesus' blood shed on the cross.
col-1-21-22: Paul reminds the Colossians that they were once far from God and hostile in mind and deed. Now Christ's physical death has reconciled them, so he can present them holy and blameless before God.
col-1-27: Paul says God has now revealed a long-hidden secret, even to Gentiles: Christ himself lives in his people, and that is their confident hope of sharing God's glory.
col-2-6-7: Paul urges believers to keep living in union with Christ, just as they began. Like trees with deep roots and buildings on firm foundations, they should grow strong in faith and overflow with thankfulness.
col-2-9-10: Countering false teachers, Paul says that the whole fullness of God lives in Christ in bodily form. Believers lack nothing spiritually, because they have been made complete in him, the head over every power.
col-2-13-14: Paul reminds believers that they were spiritually dead in sin, but God made them alive with Christ and forgave all their sins. He cancelled the record of debt against them by nailing it to the cross.
col-3-1-4: Paul urges believers, raised with Christ, to set their hearts and minds on heavenly things where Christ reigns. Their true life is now hidden with him, and when he appears they will share his glory.
col-3-12-15: Paul tells believers, as God's chosen and dearly loved people, to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. They should forgive as the Lord forgave them, and let Christ's peace rule.
col-3-16-17: Paul urges believers to let Christ's message live richly among them as they teach and sing to God with thankful hearts. Whatever they say or do should be done in Jesus' name, giving thanks.
1th-1-4-5: Paul tells the Thessalonians he knows God loves and has chosen them, because the gospel came to them not only in words but with power, the Holy Spirit and deep conviction.
1th-3-12-13: Paul prays that the Lord would make the Thessalonians' love for each other and for everyone grow and overflow. Then their hearts will be strong and blameless when Jesus returns.
1th-4-13-14: Paul writes to believers grieving for those who have died. He does not forbid grief but says they need not mourn without hope: since Jesus died and rose, God will bring the believing dead with him.
1th-4-16-18: Paul describes the Lord's return: he will come from heaven with a loud command and God's trumpet. The believing dead will rise first, then the living will join them, and all will be with the Lord for ever.
1th-5-9-10: Paul assures believers that God did not destine them for judgment but for salvation through Jesus, who died for them. Whether alive or dead when he returns, they will live together with him.
1th-5-16-18: Paul gives three short commands: always be joyful, keep praying and give thanks in every circumstance. Not for every circumstance, but in it, because this is God's will for believers.
1th-5-23-24: Paul prays that the God of peace would make believers completely holy and keep their whole being blameless until Christ returns. He adds that God, who calls them, is faithful and will do it.
2th-1-6-7: Paul tells persecuted believers that God is just. He will repay those who trouble them and give relief to the suffering when Jesus is revealed from heaven with his angels.
2th-2-13-14: Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians, loved by the Lord. God chose them to be saved through the Spirit's work and belief in the truth, calling them through the gospel to share Christ's glory.
2th-2-16-17: Paul prays that Jesus and God the Father, who loved them and gave them lasting comfort and good hope by grace, would encourage their hearts and strengthen them in everything good they say and do.
2th-3-3: Paul assures believers that, unlike unreliable people, the Lord is faithful. He will strengthen them and protect them from the evil one.
2th-3-16: Paul closes with a prayer that the Lord of peace himself would give the Thessalonians peace at all times and in every way, and that the Lord would be with them all.
1ti-1-14-15: Paul recalls how the Lord's grace overflowed to him, a former persecutor. He calls this saying trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul sees himself as the worst of them.
1ti-2-3-6: Paul tells Timothy that God our Saviour wants all people to be saved and come to know the truth. There is one God and one mediator between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.
1ti-4-8-10: Paul tells Timothy that physical training has some value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for this life and the next. That is why they work hard, hoping in the living God.
1ti-6-6-8: Warning against people who see religion as a way to get rich, Paul says true gain is godliness combined with contentment. We bring nothing into the world and take nothing out, so food and clothing are enough.
1ti-6-12: Paul urges Timothy to fight the good fight of faith and take firm hold of the eternal life God called him to, which he confessed publicly before many witnesses.
1ti-6-17-19: Paul tells Timothy to instruct wealthy believers not to be proud or trust uncertain riches, but to trust God, who generously provides all we enjoy. They should be rich in good deeds and generous.
2ti-1-7: Encouraging the timid Timothy, Paul reminds him that the Spirit God gave does not make us fearful. He gives power, love and self-discipline, so Timothy need not be ashamed of the gospel.
2ti-1-9-10: Paul reminds Timothy that God saved and called them not because of anything they did but by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began. Jesus has now destroyed death and brought life to light.
2ti-1-12: Writing from prison, Paul says he is not ashamed of his suffering, because he knows the one he has trusted. He is convinced Christ can guard what Paul has entrusted to him until the final day.
2ti-2-11-13: Paul quotes a reliable early saying: if we died with Christ we will live with him, and if we endure we will reign with him. Denying him has consequences, yet even when we are faithless, he stays faithful.
2ti-2-19: Despite false teachers, Paul says God's foundation stands firm, bearing two inscriptions: the Lord knows who belongs to him, and everyone who claims his name must turn away from wickedness.
2ti-3-15-17: Paul reminds Timothy that the Scriptures he learned as a child can make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ. All Scripture is breathed out by God and useful for teaching and correcting, equipping believers for good work.
2ti-4-7-8: Near the end of his life, Paul says he has fought well, finished the race and kept the faith. The Lord, the righteous judge, will give him a crown of righteousness, as he will all who long for his appearing.
2ti-4-17-18: Paul recalls that when everyone deserted him at his trial, the Lord stood by him and gave him strength to preach. He is confident the Lord will rescue him from every evil and bring him safely to his heavenly kingdom.
tit-1-1-2: Introducing himself to Titus, Paul says his work rests on the hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before time began.
tit-2-11-14: Paul explains that God's grace has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It trains believers to reject ungodliness and live wisely now, as they wait for Christ's return, who gave himself to make them his own.
tit-3-4-7: Paul says that when God's kindness and love appeared, he saved us because of his mercy, not our good deeds. He washed and renewed us by the Holy Spirit, so that, made right by grace, we would inherit eternal life.
phm-1-4-7: Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, and prays his generosity would deepen his understanding of every good thing in Christ. Philemon's kindness has refreshed the hearts of God's people.
heb-1-3: The writer of Hebrews describes the Son as the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of his being. He sustains everything by his word, and after cleansing sins he sat down at God's right hand.
heb-2-14-15: The writer explains that Jesus became fully human so that through his death he could break the devil's power over death. He frees those who lived their whole lives enslaved by the fear of death.
heb-2-17-18: The writer explains that Jesus became like us in every way so he could be a merciful and faithful high priest, making atonement for sins. Because he suffered when tempted, he can help those being tempted.
heb-3-6: The writer contrasts Moses, a servant in God's house, with Christ, a faithful Son over it. Believers are his house, provided they keep holding firmly to their confidence and hope.
heb-4-9-11: The writer says that a Sabbath rest still awaits God's people, a rest Joshua never fully gave Israel. Those who enter it rest from their labours, so readers should make every effort to enter, and not fall through unbelief.
heb-4-12-13: The writer warns that God's word is living and active, sharper than any sword, exposing our deepest thoughts and motives. Nothing is hidden from God, to whom we must give account.
heb-4-14-16: The writer urges readers to hold firmly to their faith, because Jesus is a great high priest who understands our weaknesses and was tempted yet never sinned. So we can approach God's throne boldly for mercy and help.
heb-6-10: After a stern warning, the writer reassures readers that God is fair and will not forget the work they have done and the love they have shown by serving fellow believers.
heb-6-17-19: The writer explains that God confirmed his promise to Abraham with an oath, so his heirs would know his purpose cannot change. Since God cannot lie, this hope is a firm, secure anchor for the soul.
heb-7-24-25: The writer explains that unlike earlier priests who died, Jesus lives for ever, so his priesthood is permanent. He can save completely those who come to God through him, because he always lives to intercede for them.
heb-8-10-12: God promised Israel through Jeremiah a new covenant: he would write his laws on their hearts, be their God and forgive their sins completely. Hebrews shows that Christ has brought this covenant into effect.
heb-9-12: The writer contrasts the yearly animal sacrifices of the high priest with Christ, who entered God's presence once for all with his own blood, securing a redemption that lasts for ever.
heb-9-14: The writer reasons that if animal blood could make people outwardly clean, Christ's blood, offered to God through the eternal Spirit, can do far more: cleanse our consciences so we can serve the living God.
heb-9-27-28: The writer explains that people die once and then face judgment. In the same way Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and he will return, not to deal with sin, but to save those waiting for him.
heb-10-14: The writer explains that by his single sacrifice Christ has made perfect for ever those who are being made holy. Nothing needs to be added to it.
heb-10-16-17: Hebrews repeats God's new covenant promise first given through Jeremiah: he will put his laws in his people's hearts and minds and will never again remember their sins. So no further sacrifice is needed.
heb-10-19-22: The writer tells believers that Jesus' blood has opened a new and living way into God's presence. With Jesus as their great priest, they should draw near to God with sincere hearts and full assurance of faith.
heb-10-23: The writer urges readers under pressure to keep holding to the hope they profess without wavering, because God, who made the promise, is faithful.
heb-10-35-36: Remembering their earlier courage under persecution, the writer urges readers not to throw away their confidence, which will be richly rewarded. They need endurance, so that after doing God's will they receive what he promised.
heb-11-1: The writer defines faith as being sure of what we hope for and convinced of realities we cannot see, introducing a long list of Old Testament examples.
heb-11-6: The writer says it is impossible to please God without faith. Anyone who comes to him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him.
heb-11-11: The writer recalls how Sarah, though long past childbearing age, received power to conceive, because she considered God faithful to keep his promise.
heb-12-1-2: Surrounded by the faithful witnesses of the past, believers should throw off every hindrance and sin and run their race with endurance. They are to fix their eyes on Jesus, who endured the cross.
heb-12-5-6: The writer reminds suffering believers of Proverbs' advice not to despise the Lord's discipline or lose heart. God disciplines those he loves, as a father corrects a child he accepts.
heb-12-10-11: The writer compares human fathers, who disciplined imperfectly for a short time, with God, who disciplines for our good so we can share his holiness. Discipline hurts at the time, but later it produces peace and righteousness.
heb-12-28: The writer says that while the created world will be shaken, believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. So they should be thankful and worship God with reverence and awe.
heb-13-5-6: The writer urges readers not to love money but to be content, quoting God's pledge never to leave or abandon his people. Because of this, believers can say with confidence that the Lord helps them and they need not fear.
heb-13-8: Urging readers to remember faithful leaders and avoid strange teachings, the writer declares that Jesus Christ does not change: he is the same yesterday, today and for ever.
heb-13-20-21: The writer closes with a blessing: may the God of peace, who raised Jesus, the great Shepherd, through the blood of the eternal covenant, equip readers with everything good to do his will, working in them what pleases him.
jas-1-2-4: James tells believers to treat trials as a reason for joy, not because suffering is good, but because testing their faith builds endurance. Endurance, allowed to finish its work, makes them mature and complete.
jas-1-5-6: James tells anyone lacking wisdom, especially in trials, to ask God, who gives generously to all without scolding. They should ask trusting him, not torn by doubt like a wave tossed by the wind.
jas-1-12: James says people who endure testing are blessed. Once they have stood the test, they will receive the crown of life, which the Lord has promised to those who love him.
jas-1-17-18: James insists that God does not tempt anyone; every good and perfect gift comes from him, the unchanging Father of the heavenly lights. By his own choice he gave believers new birth through the word of truth.
jas-1-19-20: James urges believers to be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteous life God wants.
jas-2-5: Rebuking believers who favoured the rich, James reminds them that God has chosen many of the world's poor to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised to those who love him.
jas-2-12-13: James urges believers to speak and act as people who will be judged by the law that gives freedom. There will be no mercy for those who show none, but mercy triumphs over judgment.
jas-4-6-8: James says God gives more grace, quoting Proverbs: he opposes the proud but favours the humble. So believers should submit to God and resist the devil, who will flee. As they draw near to God, he will draw near to them.
jas-4-10: After calling worldly believers to repent, James tells them to humble themselves before the Lord, and he will lift them up.
jas-5-7-8: James urges suffering believers to be patient until the Lord returns, like a farmer waiting for the autumn and spring rains. They should strengthen their hearts, because his coming is near.
jas-5-11: James points to Job as an example of endurance. Those who persevere are counted blessed, and the end of Job's story shows that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
jas-5-13-16: James tells believers to pray in trouble and sing when happy. The sick should call the elders to pray and anoint them; faithful prayer will restore them and sins will be forgiven, so they should confess and pray for one another.
1pe-1-3-5: Peter praises God, who in his mercy has given believers new birth into a living hope through Jesus' resurrection. Their inheritance is kept safe in heaven, and God's power guards them until salvation is revealed.
1pe-1-6-7: Peter says believers can rejoice even while grieving through trials for a while. Like gold refined by fire, their tested faith proves genuine and will bring praise and honour when Jesus is revealed.
1pe-1-8-9: Peter observes that his readers love Jesus though they have never seen him. Trusting him, they are filled with a joy too great for words as they receive the goal of their faith, the salvation of their souls.
1pe-1-18-19: Peter reminds believers that they were set free from the empty way of life inherited from their ancestors, not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless lamb.
1pe-1-23-25: Peter says believers have been born again through God's living, lasting word. Quoting Isaiah, he contrasts human life, which fades like grass, with the Lord's word, which endures for ever.
1pe-2-4-6: Peter describes Jesus as the living stone people rejected but God chose. Believers, like living stones, are built into a spiritual temple, and as Isaiah says, whoever trusts in him will never be put to shame.
1pe-2-9-10: Peter applies Israel's titles to believers: they are a chosen people, royal priests, a holy nation belonging to God. Once they were not a people and had no mercy; now they are God's people and have received mercy.
1pe-2-24-25: Peter tells believers that Christ carried their sins in his body on the cross so they could die to sin and live for what is right. By his wounds they are healed, and they have returned to their Shepherd.
1pe-3-8-9: Peter urges believers to be united, sympathetic, loving, compassionate and humble. Instead of repaying evil or insult, they should bless, because that is their calling and they will inherit a blessing.
1pe-3-12: Peter quotes Psalm 34: the Lord watches over those who do right and listens to their prayers, but he sets himself against those who do evil.
1pe-3-18: Peter explains that Christ suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring people to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive by the Spirit.
1pe-4-12-13: Peter tells believers not to be surprised by fiery trials, as if something strange were happening. They should rejoice to share Christ's sufferings, so they will be overjoyed when his glory is revealed.
1pe-4-19: Peter concludes that those who suffer for doing what is right, as God allows, should entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.
1pe-5-6-7: Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God's powerful hand, so he can lift them up at the right time. They can give all their worries to God, because he cares for them.
1pe-5-8-10: Peter warns believers to stay alert, because the devil prowls like a roaring lion. They should resist him firmly, knowing others suffer too, and after a little while the God of all grace will restore and strengthen them.
2pe-1-3-4: Peter says God's power has given believers everything they need for a godly life through knowing him. Through his great promises they can share in his nature and escape the world's corruption.
2pe-1-10-11: Peter urges believers to work hard to confirm God's call by growing in faith, goodness and love. Then they will not stumble and will receive a rich welcome into Christ's eternal kingdom.
2pe-3-8-9: Answering scoffers who say Christ's return is delayed, Peter says God does not measure time as we do. He is not slow in keeping his promise but patient, wanting no one to perish and everyone to repent.
2pe-3-13: Peter says that, based on God's promise, believers look forward to new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home.
1jn-1-5-7: John says that God is light with no darkness at all, so claiming fellowship with him while living in darkness is a lie. If we live in the light, we have fellowship with each other and Jesus' blood cleanses us from all sin.
1jn-1-8-9: John warns that claiming to be without sin is self-deception. But if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just: he will forgive us and cleanse us from all wrongdoing.
1jn-2-1-2: John writes so that believers will not sin, but if they do, Jesus the Righteous One speaks to the Father on their behalf. He is the sacrifice that takes away our sins, and not only ours, but the whole world's.
1jn-2-12: John tells his readers, whom he calls dear children, that he writes because their sins have been forgiven for the sake of Jesus' name.
1jn-2-17: John warns against loving the world. The world and its desires are passing away, but whoever does God's will lives for ever.
1jn-2-25: John reminds believers to hold on to what they heard from the beginning, because what God has promised them is eternal life.
1jn-3-1-2: John marvels at the Father's great love in calling us his children, which is what we are. What we will become is not yet clear, but when Christ appears we will be like him, for we will see him as he is.
1jn-3-8: John says that those who keep on sinning belong to the devil, who has sinned from the beginning. The Son of God appeared precisely to destroy the devil's work.
1jn-3-16: John says we know what love is because Jesus gave his life for us. So we too should be willing to give our lives for our fellow believers.
1jn-3-19-20: John tells believers that showing love in action reassures them they belong to the truth. Even when their conscience condemns them, God is greater than their hearts and knows everything.
1jn-3-21-22: John says that when our conscience is clear, we can come to God confidently, and we receive what we ask because we obey him and do what pleases him.
1jn-4-4: John tells believers that they belong to God and have overcome the false prophets, because the Spirit who lives in them is greater than the spirit at work in the world.
1jn-4-7-10: John urges believers to love one another, because love comes from God and God is love. God showed his love by sending his Son as the sacrifice for our sins, not because we loved him first.
1jn-4-16-18: John says that God is love, and whoever lives in love lives in God. As his love matures in us, we can face judgment day with confidence, because perfect love drives out fear of punishment.
1jn-4-19: John explains that our love for God and others is a response: we love because God first loved us.
1jn-5-4-5: John says that everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory comes through faith. Those who overcome are those who believe that Jesus is the Son of God.
1jn-5-11-13: John states God's testimony: he has given us eternal life, and this life is found in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life, and John writes so believers can know they have eternal life.
1jn-5-14-15: John says believers can approach God confidently: if they ask anything that fits his will, he hears them. And if he hears them, they can be sure he grants what they ask.
1jn-5-18: John says that those born of God do not keep on sinning, because Jesus, the one born of God, keeps them safe, and the evil one cannot harm them.
2jn-1-2-3: The elder writes to a church he loves in the truth that lives in them for ever. He assures them that grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and Jesus will be with them in truth and love.
3jn-1-2: The elder tells his friend Gaius that he prays his health and circumstances may go as well as his soul is already going. It is a personal wish for a friend, not a promise of prosperity.
jud-1-1: Jude greets his readers as people called by God, loved by the Father and kept safe for Jesus Christ.
jud-1-20-21: Jude urges believers, surrounded by false teachers, to build themselves up in their faith and pray in the Holy Spirit. They should keep themselves in God's love as they wait for Jesus' mercy that brings eternal life.
jud-1-24-25: Jude ends with praise to God, who is able to keep believers from falling and to bring them into his glorious presence without fault and with great joy. All glory and power belong to him for ever.
rev-1-3: At the start of Revelation, John pronounces a blessing on those who read this prophecy aloud, and on those who hear it and take it to heart, because the time is near.
rev-1-5-6: John greets the churches from Jesus, the faithful witness and first to rise from the dead. He praises Jesus, who loves us, freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom of priests to serve God.
rev-1-17-18: When John fell at the feet of the glorified Jesus as though dead, Jesus touched him and told him not to be afraid. He is the First and the Last, who died and now lives for ever, holding the keys of death and the grave.
rev-2-7: Jesus promises, in his message to the church in Ephesus, that everyone who overcomes will be allowed to eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.
rev-2-10: Jesus told the persecuted church in Smyrna not to fear what they were about to suffer, including prison. If they stayed faithful even to death, he would give them the crown of life.
rev-2-11: Jesus promises, in his message to Smyrna, that whoever overcomes will not be harmed by the second death, the final judgment beyond physical death.
rev-2-17: Jesus promises, in his message to Pergamum, that those who overcome will receive hidden manna, true spiritual food, and a white stone bearing a new name known only to the one who receives it.
rev-2-26-28: Jesus promises, writing to Thyatira, that whoever overcomes and keeps doing his will to the end will share his authority over the nations, as he received it from the Father, and will receive the morning star.
rev-3-5: Jesus promises, in his message to Sardis, that those who overcome will be dressed in white, their names will never be erased from the book of life, and he will acknowledge them before his Father and the angels.
rev-3-8: Jesus told the small, weak church in Philadelphia that he knew their faithfulness. Because they had kept his word and not denied him, he had set before them an open door that no one could shut.
rev-3-10: Jesus told the church in Philadelphia that because they had patiently endured as he commanded, he would keep them through the coming hour of trial that would test the whole world.
rev-3-11-12: Jesus promises that whoever overcomes will be a permanent pillar in God's temple, bearing God's name and his own. He is coming soon, so the church must hold on so no one takes their crown.
rev-3-19-21: Jesus tells the lukewarm church in Laodicea that he corrects those he loves, so they should repent. He stands knocking, ready to share a meal with anyone who opens, and overcomers will sit with him on his throne.
rev-5-9-10: In John's vision, heavenly worshippers sing a new song to the Lamb. He is worthy because he was slain and with his blood bought people from every nation to be a kingdom of priests who will reign on the earth.
rev-7-9-10: John sees a vast crowd no one could count, from every nation and language, standing before God's throne and the Lamb in white robes. They cry out that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb.
rev-7-15-17: An elder explains to John that those who came through great suffering now serve before God's throne. God will shelter them, they will never hunger or thirst again, and the Lamb will lead them to living water and wipe away every tear.
rev-11-15: When the seventh angel blows his trumpet, loud voices in heaven announce that the world's kingdom now belongs to our Lord and his Messiah, who will reign for ever and ever.
rev-12-10-11: A loud voice in heaven announces that God's salvation and kingdom have come, because Satan, who accused believers day and night, has been thrown down. They overcame him by the Lamb's blood and their testimony, even unto death.
rev-14-12-13: John is told that this calls for endurance from God's faithful people. A voice from heaven declares those who die in the Lord blessed, and the Spirit adds that they will rest from their labours, their deeds following them.
rev-19-6-7: John hears a huge crowd, loud as rushing waters and thunder, shouting "Hallelujah!" because the Lord God Almighty reigns. They rejoice because the wedding of the Lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready.
rev-19-9: An angel tells John to write that those invited to the Lamb's wedding feast are blessed, adding that these are the true words of God.
rev-20-6: John declares blessed and holy those who share in the first resurrection. The second death has no power over them, and they will serve as priests of God and Christ and reign with him.
rev-21-1-2: John sees a new heaven and a new earth replacing the old, with no more sea. The holy city, the New Jerusalem, comes down from God, beautiful like a bride dressed for her husband.
rev-21-3-4: A loud voice from the throne announces that God's home is now among his people, and he will live with them. He will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying and pain will be gone for ever.
rev-21-5-7: God promises, seated on the throne, that he is making everything new and that his words are trustworthy. He will freely give the water of life to the thirsty, and those who overcome will inherit all this as his children.
rev-21-23-25: John describes the New Jerusalem as needing no sun or moon, because God's glory gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp. The nations will walk by its light, and its gates will never close, because there is no night.
rev-21-26-27: John says the nations will bring their glory and honour into the city, but nothing impure and no one who practises deceit or shameful things will enter. Only those written in the Lamb's book of life will be there.
rev-22-1-2: An angel shows John a crystal-clear river of the water of life flowing from God's throne down the city's street. The tree of life grows on both banks, bearing fruit every month, and its leaves heal the nations.
rev-22-3-5: John says there will be no more curse in the city. God's servants will serve him, see his face and bear his name. There will be no night, because the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign for ever.
rev-22-12: Jesus promises that he is coming soon. He brings his reward with him and will repay each person according to what they have done.
rev-22-14: Jesus pronounces a blessing on those who obey God's commands (some manuscripts read "wash their robes"). They will have the right to eat from the tree of life and enter the city through its gates.
rev-22-16: Jesus confirms that he sent his angel to give this message to the churches. He calls himself both the root and the descendant of David, the promised king, and the bright morning star.
rev-22-17: Near the end of Revelation, the Spirit and the church, Christ's bride, call out "Come!" Everyone who is thirsty and willing is invited to take the water of life as a free gift.
rev-22-20: Jesus promises, in the Bible's closing lines, that he is coming soon. John answers with the longing of the whole church: "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!"
